# Nomana-IT Documentation — full text for LLMs

> Documentation of the software published by Nomana-IT, a software publisher and JD Edwards / Oracle / AI consultancy. Liberty Next is a low-code application platform; Nomaflow (scheduling and orchestration), Nomasx-1 (security, licence compliance and segregation of duties) and Nomajde (JD Edwards EnterpriseOne companion) are built with and for Liberty Next. NomaUBL is a standalone e-invoicing platform for the French reform (UBL, Plateforme Agréée, e-reporting). The site also documents open-source JD Edwards and BI Publisher APIs. Liberty Next and NomaUBL include built-in AI assistants, powered by Claude (Anthropic), that answer from the documentation and from the data of the instance.

Company: https://nomana-it.fr/ · AI services: https://nomana-it.fr/ai/ · Index: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/llms.txt · French: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/llms-full.fr.txt

# === Products — overviews and getting started ===

## Liberty Next — Getting Started
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/getting-started/

Liberty Next — connector-driven low-code framework. Configuration drives discovery: define a SQL or API connector in TOML, expose its queries to a screen or a dashboard, and the React UI builds the grid, the form and the filters automatically.

**Liberty Next** is a connector-driven low-code framework. The principle is simple: **configuration describes the data sources, the framework discovers the rest at runtime.** A SQL connector is a few lines of TOML pointing at a database pool and a list of queries; the React UI then builds a typed grid, a filter row, a modal form and lookups from the columns the query actually returns — no schema duplication, no per-screen code.

Two paid applications ship on Liberty Next:

- **[Nomasx-1](/liberty/nomasx1/overview)** — enterprise security and compliance. Centralised view of users and roles, Oracle and JD Edwards licence compliance, automated Segregation of Duties analysis. For auditors, security officers and licence managers.
- **[Nomajde](/liberty/nomajde/overview)** — JD Edwards companion. Live screens on the JDE data: master data, security maintenance workbench, transactions, scheduled BIP reporting, live monitoring. For JDE operators, security administrators and ops engineers.

The framework itself (without the licensed connectors) is free.

:::info[Active development]
Liberty Next is under active development — new capabilities ship regularly, and this documentation tracks the framework as it evolves. The [Framework](./framework/overview.md) section is the recommended entry point.
:::

## At a glance

---

## What it brings

| Area | What Liberty Next provides |
|---|---|
| **Data sources** | SQL pools (PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQLite) and HTTP API endpoints, declared in TOML under `config/`. |
| **Schema discovery** | Columns are read from the query's cursor at runtime; the dictionary adds labels, formats and display rules per column. |
| **Screens** | One [`Screen`](./framework/build/screens/overview.md) entry per business object: grid, modal form, per-field conditions, audit tab. |
| **Dashboards** | [Charts and KPIs](./framework/dashboards.md) over the same named queries — bar, line, pie, stat panels. |
| **Auth** | TOML or database backend, JWT tokens, OIDC against any provider. |
| **AI assistant** | Anthropic-powered tool-use over the connectors, screens and dashboards configured on the instance. |
| **Frontend** | React 19 + Vite + TypeScript, single-page, dark default with light theme, EN / FR. |

---

## Local development

```bash
python3.12 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -e ".[dev]"

./start.sh init-config    # copy config/*.toml.example → real (uncommitted) files
./start.sh init-db        # FIRST RUN: create the auth store + an `admin` user
./start.sh                # build frontend if stale, then run FastAPI on :8000
./start.sh dev            # same, with auto-reload
./start.sh frontend       # Vite dev server on :5173 (HMR) — pair with `./start.sh api dev`
./start.sh help           # all commands
```

The backend serves the built frontend (`frontend/dist`) at `/`; no copy step. A fresh checkout with no `config/connectors.toml` runs API-only — the framework pool is the only connector configured by default.

Environment knobs:

| Variable | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `LIBERTY_DB_URL` | The framework's own database. Defaults to a local SQLite file. |
| `LIBERTY_JWT_SECRET` | Token signing key — ephemeral when unset. |
| `LIBERTY_MASTER_KEY` | Crypto master key used to decrypt `ENC:` values in configuration. |
| `LIBERTY_LICENSE_KEY` | RS256-signed JWT that unlocks licensed connectors (nomasx1 / nomajde). |
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | Enables the in-app AI assistant. |

Config files support `${NAME}` and `${NAME:-default}` references.

## Why Liberty Framework
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/overview/

Liberty Framework is a low-code platform for building internal applications — admin tools, BI dashboards, integration glue, customer portals — without writing a frontend. Define data sources and screens in the Settings UI; the framework renders the grid, the edit dialog, the dashboard, the assistant.

You have a database. Or a JD Edwards instance. Or a SaaS API your team needs to talk to. And what you want is a **clean, fast internal interface** to look at that data, edit it, drill into it, schedule things against it — without spending three months writing a React app for each one.

That's what Liberty Framework is for.

You install it once, point it at your data source, and define **what people should see** through a Settings UI: which queries feed which screens, which screens belong to which menu, which dashboards aggregate what. The framework handles everything else — rendering the grid, the edit dialog, the filters, the authentication, the role pruning, the export buttons, the audit columns, the assistant, the scheduled jobs.

A handful of concepts (a *pool*, a *connector*, a *screen*, a *dashboard*, a *menu*) compose to cover the surface most internal applications need: CRUD over databases, KPIs and charts, role-gated access, ETL pipelines, an AI assistant that can run your queries on demand.

---

## What problem it solves

Most teams end up writing the same kind of application over and over:

- **A grid that lists rows from a table**, with filters and pagination.
- **An edit dialog** that opens when you click a row, with the form fields the database carries.
- **A dashboard** with a few KPIs and charts on top of the same data.
- **A menu** that ties everything together.
- **Authentication** so only the right people see the right things.

Writing this in React (or Angular, or Vue) is a week of work per screen. Multiply by 20 screens per app, and 5 apps per team, and the math is brutal — most of the engineering hours go into wiring forms to APIs and APIs to databases, with very little of it surfacing as actual business logic.

The framework takes the opposite stance: the **schema** of every query is discovered at runtime from the database itself, the **layout** is described in a few clicks in the Settings UI, and the **rendering** — grid, dialog, dashboard, AI tool, REST surface — is the framework's job, not yours. You write SQL. You get a UI.

When something the framework doesn't cover comes up (a custom widget, a one-off page, a hand-tuned UX) the platform stays out of the way — you can wire in a React route, a custom Python step, or a raw HTTP endpoint.

---

## Who it's for

| Audience | Why they pick the framework |
|---|---|
| **Internal-tools teams** building admin apps over existing databases. | The CRUD-screen path is six clicks away; no time spent re-inventing it. |
| **JD Edwards / SAP / NetSuite operators** who need to administer their ERP from a modern UI without waiting on the vendor. | Connect to the ERP's pool, expose the right queries, drop a screen on top. |
| **BI / analytics teams** consolidating reports across systems. | Dashboards over named SQL queries, charts that reuse the data, no separate BI tool needed. |
| **Integration teams** that need a UI on top of data loads and scheduled jobs. | Nomaflow runs the jobs, the framework gives them a UI; the AI assistant calls the same queries on demand. |
| **Software vendors** packaging customer-facing apps on top of a database product. | The framework is the chassis; you ship per-customer configuration as a portable zip. |

It's **less interesting** for:

- Public-facing consumer apps (the framework's UX is operator-oriented).
- Mobile apps (the SPA works on mobile but isn't built mobile-first).
- One-off marketing sites or content management — there are simpler tools.

---

## What makes it different

| Most low-code tools | Liberty Framework |
|---|---|
| Drag-and-drop form designer that generates a custom UI per page. | One coherent UI grammar — a grid + a dialog — applied across every screen. Faster to learn for users, faster to build for developers. |
| Proprietary backend that owns your data. | Your own database. Your own pool. The framework only reaches it through declared queries; export and migration are trivial. |
| You're tied to the vendor's hosting. | Self-hosted. systemd, Docker, Kubernetes — your call. |
| Schema declared by hand in the tool. | Schema discovered at runtime from the live query. Change the SQL, the UI follows. |
| Closed plugin model. | Open Python plugins, custom React routes, REST API, and a tool-use AI assistant that runs the same queries as the UI. |
| You pick a stack and learn it. | You already know SQL; the rest is checkboxes and dropdowns. |

The most important difference is the **schema-discovered** model: nothing about your data is duplicated in framework configuration. The connector knows the query; the database knows the columns. When a column changes, the UI reflects it on the next reload.

---

## Five concepts, one mental model

Everything the framework does is composed from five concepts:

| Concept | What it is | What it solves |
|---|---|---|
| **[Pool](./connectors.md#pools)** | A connection to a database (a SQLAlchemy URL + credentials). | "How do I reach this data?" |
| **[Connector](./connectors.md)** | A named set of queries / endpoints on top of a pool. | "What questions do I want to ask this data source?" |
| **[Screen](./build/screens/overview.md)** | A grid + edit dialog over a connector's queries. | "How do I let a person look at this and edit it?" |
| **[Dashboard](./dashboards.md)** | A layout of KPIs and charts over the same queries. | "How do I summarise this for someone who just wants the headline?" |
| **[Menu](./build/menus/overview.md)** | The sidebar tree that organises screens and dashboards into an app. | "How do I make this navigable?" |

Around those five sit the supporting layers: the [dictionary](./dictionary.md) for labels and formats, [authentication & roles](./build/secure/sign-in.md) for who-sees-what, [jobs](../nomaflow/overview.md) for scheduled work, [AI assistant](./ai-assistant.md) for natural-language access, [plugins](./apps/plugins.md) for custom Python.

Every concept page on this site opens with **what it is, why it exists, when you create one, how it fits with the others**. Once you've read those five, the framework's surface is essentially mapped.

## How to learn it

Three paths into the framework — pick whichever suits how you read.

### 1. Hands-on tutorials *(recommended)*

The **[Build a CRM tutorial](./tutorial-crm/01-setup.md)** is a six-step walkthrough that produces a working customer-relationship-management application — customers, deals, activities, a sales-pipeline dashboard, OIDC sign-in, role-based access, the AI assistant and a scheduled job. The domain is generic; no prior knowledge needed beyond SQL.

For a real-world ERP admin built on the framework, the packaged **[Nomajde](../nomajde/overview.md)** app covers JD Edwards end-to-end out of the box — users, roles, security workbench, BIP queue, master data. Install it, point it at your JDE database, get a working admin without building anything yourself.

### 2. Use-case-driven

If you'd rather start from *what you want to build*, the **[What you can build](./what-you-can-build.md)** page lists every common use case (internal CRUD, admin tools, BI dashboards, integration glue, customer portals, workflow orchestration, ETL) with a one-paragraph "how the framework does it" plus a link to the relevant tutorial / cookbook recipe.

### 3. Reference-first

If you're the type who reads documentation top-to-bottom, the **[Getting Started](../installation/python-server.md)** section walks you through installation, the file layout, the Settings UI; then the **Concepts** section explains each primitive in depth.

---

## Frontend in one paragraph

React 19 + Vite + TypeScript, built once into `frontend/dist` and served as static by the FastAPI backend on the same port. Dark default with a light theme swap, `react-i18next` EN / FR, `lucide-react` icons, DM Sans, `@tanstack/react-table` for the grid, `react-markdown` + `remark-gfm` for the assistant, `@monaco-editor/react` for the in-app code editing. You don't write any of it — the framework renders everything off the configuration.

---

## Backend in one paragraph

Python 3.12, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy 2.0 async with asyncpg (PostgreSQL) + oracledb (Oracle, thin), Anthropic SDK for the AI assistant, authlib for OIDC, Argon2 for password hashing, cryptography for AES-256-GCM field encryption, APScheduler for cron jobs, Socket.IO for live updates. One process, one port, no companion daemons. Python is only written for a custom job step or screen action.

## Liberty Next — What you can build
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/what-you-can-build/

What teams build with Liberty Next — admin apps over existing tables, dashboards, an interface over an ERP database, integration and data-loading jobs, workflows with conditional forms — with what the framework provides, what is left to configure, and when another tool fits better.

Liberty Next combines a few building blocks — connectors and their queries, screens, menus, dashboards, jobs, roles — configured from Settings. This page lists what teams build with them, what each case relies on, and where to start.

The pattern is always the same: **connect the database, write the queries, build the screens, organise the menu, set the roles**.

---

## 1. Admin apps over existing tables \{#admin\}

A database (customers, products, contracts, tickets…) and a team that must read, filter, edit and export it.

| Provided | Where |
|---|---|
| Grid with sorting, filters, grouping and saved views | [Screens](./build/screens/overview.md), [Saved views](./saved-views.md) |
| Edit dialog with tabs, lists of values, conditional fields | [Dialog builder](./build/screens/dialog-builder.md), [Form conditions](./form-conditions.md) |
| Add / edit / delete, in the dialog or in the grid, with Excel / CSV import | [Screens](./build/screens/overview.md) |
| Excel export | [Excel export](./cookbook/excel-export.md) |
| Audit columns filled by the server (`LOGIN`, `SYSDATE`) and a history table (`audit_table`) | [Dictionary](./dictionary.md#rules), [Audit trail](./cookbook/audit-trail.md) |
| Record locks: two users cannot edit the same row at once | [Monitoring](../monitoring/dashboard.md) |
| Interface in English and French, translated labels | [i18n](./apps/i18n.md) |

**To configure**: the pool, the queries (the CRUD wizard writes them from a table), the screens and the menu. Most of the time goes into the SQL.

**Start with**: [Tutorial — Build a CRM](./tutorial-crm/01-setup.md), or [CRUD over an existing table](./cookbook/crud-existing-table.md) for a single screen.

---

## 2. Dashboards \{#dashboards\}

| Provided | Where |
|---|---|
| KPI, chart (bar, line, area, pie) and table widgets on a 12-column grid | [Dashboards](./dashboards.md), [Charts](./charts.md) |
| A period with presets, and the change compared with the previous period | [Dashboards](./dashboards.md) |
| Filters from the dictionary, shared by every widget | [Dashboards](./dashboards.md) |
| A cache with a **Refresh** button | [Dashboards](./dashboards.md) |
| Free analysis by the users themselves — pivot, charts, drill, calculated fields, saved analyses, Excel / PDF export | [Data Explorer](./explorer/overview.md) |

**To configure**: the aggregate queries (usually `GROUP BY` on the period), then the widgets.

**Start with**: [Tutorial — CRM → Dashboard](./tutorial-crm/04-dashboard.md).

---

## 3. An interface over an ERP database \{#erp\}

A faster interface for the ERP's operators, reading and writing its database without changing the ERP.

| Provided | Where |
|---|---|
| Oracle, SQL Server and PostgreSQL pools; Oracle thick mode for older servers | [Connectors](./connectors.md#oracle-thick) |
| One app on several environments (development, test, production) through a **Pool** picker | [Connectors → Multi-pool](./connectors.md#multi-pool) |
| JD Edwards conventions: Julian dates, right-justified codes, data dictionary import | [Dictionary](./dictionary.md#formats), [Scan a table](./dictionary.md#scan-a-table) |
| Read-only screens, writes enabled screen by screen | [Screens](./build/screens/overview.md) |

For JD Edwards, the ready-made apps cover the common needs: [Nomajde](../nomajde/overview.md) for administration and master data, [Nomasx-1](../nomasx1/overview.md) for security analysis over any connected application. For another ERP, the [CRM tutorial](./tutorial-crm/01-setup.md) shows the pattern: point the pool at the database and write the queries.

## 4. Integration and data loading \{#integration\}

[Nomaflow](../nomaflow/overview.md) runs scheduled or manual jobs made of steps.

| Provided | Where |
|---|---|
| Jobs on a cron schedule or run by hand, with retries (fixed or exponential wait) and a timeout | [Schedules](../nomaflow/jobs/schedules.md), [Steps](../nomaflow/steps.md#retry) |
| Steps: SQL query, SQL copy between databases, file load, HTTP call, LDAP sync, Python, call of another job | [Steps](../nomaflow/steps.md) |
| API connectors with Basic, Bearer, API key or OAuth2 authentication | [Connectors](./connectors.md) |
| Run history per step, live log | [Run history](../nomaflow/runs/history.md) |
| Notifications on failure, success or a missed schedule — in the app, by e-mail, or through a connector | [Notifications](../nomaflow/notifications.md) |

**To configure**: the source and target connectors, then the job's steps. Python only for what the steps cannot express — see [Plugins](./apps/plugins.md).

**Start with**: [Getting started with Nomaflow](../nomaflow/getting-started.md).

---

## 5. Apps for outside users \{#portals\}

An app opened to users outside the team, each seeing only their own rows.

| Provided | Where |
|---|---|
| Sign-in through an OpenID Connect provider | [Sign-in](./build/secure/sign-in.md), [OIDC SSO](./cookbook/oidc-sso.md) |

| Data scope: rows filtered by user attributes, applied by the server | [Row-level access](./cookbook/row-level-access.md) |
| Queries filtered on the signed-in user with `{{LOGIN}}` | [Parameter binding](./build/queries/parameter-binding.md#tokens) |
| App name, colours and fonts | Settings → Theme |

## 6. Workflows \{#workflow\}

Approve, reject, escalate: a status column and screens that adapt to it.

| Provided | Where |
|---|---|
| Fields shown, required or locked depending on the status | [Form conditions](./form-conditions.md) |
| Rows read-only once closed (`editable_when`) | [Form conditions](./form-conditions.md#editable-when) |
| Buttons running queries, with confirmation and a prompt for a reason | [Actions and lifecycle](./build/screens/actions-and-lifecycle.md) |
| Notifications when a screen writes a row, or from an action | [Notifications](../nomaflow/notifications.md) |
| Reminder jobs on a schedule | [Nomaflow](../nomaflow/overview.md) |

**Start with**: [Multi-step form](./cookbook/multi-step-form.md).

---

## When another tool fits better

- **Consumer-facing apps.** The grid-and-dialog interface is made for operators.
- **Mobile-first apps.** The application works on a tablet but is designed for a desktop screen.
- **Real-time co-editing.** Record locks prevent conflicting edits; there is no shared live editing.
- **Screens with a unique layout** (Kanban board, Gantt chart, map): the grid-and-dialog model does not suit them.

Liberty Next fits when **most screens list and edit data from a database**, with dashboards, jobs and integrations around them.

## What is Nomaflow
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomaflow/overview/

Nomaflow is the job scheduler built into Liberty Next: cron-scheduled jobs made of steps (SQL, file loads, Python, HTTP, LDAP, other jobs), retries, a run history with logs, missed-schedule detection and notifications — no separate worker or broker.

**Nomaflow** is the job scheduler built into Liberty Next. It runs inside the server — no separate worker, no message broker — and uses the same connectors as the screens and dashboards. A job is a list of **steps** run in order, on a schedule or on demand; every run is recorded with its steps and its log.

---

## At a glance

---

## What it is used for \{#uses\}

| Need | With Nomaflow |
|---|---|
| Copy a table every night from a production database to a reporting database | A `sql_copy` step, scheduled at 02:00. See [Scheduled sync](./workflows/scheduled-sync.md). |
| Load monthly spreadsheets into a facts table, replaying a wrong month | A `file_load` step in `replace_partition` mode, a refuse query for closed periods. See [Steps](./steps.md#file-load). |
| Pick up files dropped in a shared folder | `file_load` with a watched folder: each file is loaded, then moved to `done/` or `failed/`. |
| Pull data from a REST API | A `python` step that calls the API and writes through a connector's query. See [API pull](./workflows/api-pull.md). |
| Mirror Active Directory users into a table | An `ldap_sync` step. |
| Purge old rows past a threshold | A `python` step that counts and deletes. See [Conditional cleanup](./workflows/conditional-cleanup.md). |
| Run a one-off after a release | A job without a schedule, run with **Run now**. |
| Be told when a job fails or did not run | A notification rule on `failure` and `missed`. See [Notifications](./notifications.md). |

---

## How it fits in Liberty Next \{#framework\}

| Liberty Next piece | Used by Nomaflow for |
|---|---|
| Connectors and pools | Reaching the databases and APIs, through the same named queries and endpoints as the screens. |
| `jobs.toml` | The jobs, their presets and the policies — edited from the Jobs pages, carried by packages and by the licensed apps. |
| The framework database | The run history. |
| Encrypted secrets | Pool passwords; other secrets written as `${VARIABLE}` in `jobs.toml`. |
| Notifications | Telling people about failed, missed or long runs. |
| Superuser access | The Jobs pages and their API are reserved to superusers. |

---

## What it does not do \{#limits\}

- **No graph of tasks.** Steps run one after the other; a job can call another job (`call_job`) and wait for it, but nothing runs in parallel inside a job.
- **One server.** The scheduler runs in the server process: run a single instance.
- **No automatic catch-up.** A time missed while the server was down is recorded as **MISSED** and can be notified; running it again is a manual decision.
- **No replay button.** To run again with the same values, save them as a preset or pick them again in **Run with parameters**.

## Nomaflow — Getting started
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomaflow/getting-started/

A first Nomaflow job in a few minutes: open the Jobs page, create a job, add a sql_query step, set a schedule, run it by hand and read the run.

A first job: refresh a summary table every night, then run it by hand to check it.

---

## At a glance

---

## Before you start \{#before\}

- A **superuser** account — the Jobs pages are reserved to superusers.
- A SQL connector with a **write query** that does the work, for instance `daily_summary_refresh` (`INSERT … SELECT …`, `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW …`, `CALL …`). A step calls a named query of a connector, not SQL typed in the job. See [Create a custom query](../framework/build/queries/create-custom.md).

---

## 1 — Open the Jobs page \{#open\}

Open **Jobs** from the Nomaflow menu (address `/nomaflow`). Each job is a card; the toolbar has **+ New job** and **Schedule**. See [Jobs page](./jobs/catalog.md).

## 2 — Create the job \{#create\}

**+ New job**. In the **Job** section: **Id** `daily-summary`, a **Description**, the tag `reporting`, **Enabled** on.

## 3 — Add a step \{#step\}

In **Steps**, the **Add step:** bar: click `sql_query`. Give the step a **Step name** (`refresh-summary`), pick the **Connector**, then the **Query** `daily_summary_refresh`.

## 4 — Set the schedule \{#schedule\}

Back in the **Job** section: **Schedule (cron)** `0 2 * * *`, **Timezone** `Europe/Paris`. **Next runs** lists the next five nights — check them. Then **Save** at the top: the job appears on the Jobs page with its next run.

## 5 — Run it by hand \{#run\}

On the card, **▶ Run now**. The card shows the run in progress, then *last SUCCEEDED*; click it to open the run detail: the summary, the step with its state, the rows affected and the log. See [Run history](./runs/history.md).

## 6 — Be told when it fails \{#notify\}

In **Settings → Notifications**, add a rule: trigger *A job event*, job `daily-summary`, events `failure` and `missed`, channel `email`, recipient `role:ops`. See [Notifications](./notifications.md).

---

## What next \{#next\}

- More step types — loading files, copying tables, calling an API: [Steps](./steps.md).
- Run the same job with different parameters on several schedules: [Schedulable presets](./jobs/schedules.md#schedulable-presets).
- Ready-made patterns: [Workflow recipes](./workflows/scheduled-sync.md).

The teams who need to answer compliance questions never look at the same screen.     Without a unified view

Nomasx-1 replaces the spreadsheets, the manual exports and the once-a-year scramble with a continuous picture maintained by the product itself.

## The problem Nomajde solves

JD Edwards is a depth product. Most day-to-day tasks — add a user, attach a role, update a UDC value, schedule a BIP report — require navigating between five or six forms, sometimes across the fat client and the web client. Operators get the job done; they spend twice the time they should.

  
    Form ping-pong
    Five forms to onboard one user
    Create the user in P0092, set the password in the security workbench, attach the roles in P95921, pick the environments in P0093, copy the security from a reference user — each form on its own, with its own data check.
  
  
    Bulk edits hurt
    No way to edit 200 UDC values at once
    JDE forms are one-row-at-a-time editors. When the SI delivers a new module with 200 UDC values, the operator types them in by hand — or hacks together a SQL script and hopes nothing breaks.
  
  
    Reporting is its own world
    BIP runs leave no trail
    Scheduling a BIP report goes through the JDE scheduler, the output lives wherever the printer queue dropped it, and the audit of "who ran what, when" is left to the operator's memory.
  

Nomajde replaces the form ping-pong with one screen per topic, the one-row-at-a-time editor with grid editing and Excel upload, and the unwritten audit trail with a logged history of every run and every change.

Every screen writes back to JDE — no staging copy, no replay.

## NomaUBL — The unified e-invoicing platform
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/nomaubl/getting-started/

NomaUBL bridges any ERP to the French e-invoicing reform — UBL generation, pre-submission validation, Plateforme-Agréée routing, lifecycle tracking and operations on a single platform. Source-agnostic, PA-agnostic, ready for the 2026 RFE.

# NomaUBL

  French e-invoicing reform · 2026 wave
  Bridge any ERP to theFrench e-invoicing reform.
  NomaUBL is the unified platform that sits between your accounting system and the Plateforme Agréée. It generates compliant UBL from any ERP, pre-validates every invoice against XSD, Schematron and the French CTC extension, transmits to any approved platform, and tracks every invoice through its full lifecycle — submission, dispute, payment, cancellation.
  
    JD Edwards · SAP · NetSuite · Custom ERP
    EN 16931 + extended-ctc-fr
    Pluggable Plateforme Agréée
    Self-service operations
  
  
    Configure your environment →
    Tour the application
  

---

## The challenge — and why a PA alone is not enough

The French *Réforme de la Facturation Électronique* (RFE) makes structured e-invoicing **mandatory** for all B2B transactions. Companies must:

- **Generate** structured UBL invoices that comply with EN 16931 + the French CTC extension.
- **Transmit** them to their customer's Plateforme Agréée — the new state-supervised invoice rail.
- **Declare** B2C, intra-EU and out-of-scope transactions for VAT through the e-reporting flow.
- **Track** every invoice's lifecycle until it is paid, disputed, refused or cancelled.

A Plateforme Agréée handles the **transmission rail** — but not the upstream pipeline. The accounting team is still left to **produce a compliant UBL document from a non-compliant ERP output**, **detect rejections before submission**, **route by document type**, and **operate** disputes, retries, payment notifications and audit trails.

  
    Without pre-validation
    Rejection cycles — and you still pay for them
    A Plateforme Agréée bills per invoice transmitted — accepted or rejected. Every Schematron error caught downstream means a rejected invoice, a manual fix, a re-submission, a delay in cash collection — and a transmission charge. Pre-validation eliminates the round-trip and its cost.
  
  
    Without an operations layer
    Lifecycle blind spots
    Refusals, disputes and recovery codes require finance-team action. The PA records them — your operations don't see them.
  
  
    Without source flexibility
    Vendor lock-in
    An ERP-specific add-on ties you to one vendor. A custom build ties you to one team. Both fail when the regulation evolves.
  

---

## What NomaUBL is

NomaUBL is a **single-tenant, on-premise platform** that owns the entire pipeline between your accounting system and the Plateforme Agréée. It is the layer where invoices are **generated, validated, sent, tracked and recovered** — independent of which ERP produced them and which PA accepts them.

## The full pipeline, on one platform

A single NomaUBL deployment covers every step from the raw ERP output to a tracked, paid invoice:

  
    01
    
    Extract
    archive · FTP/SFTP · BIP
  

  
    02
    
    Transform
    XSLT · BIP RTF→XSL · burst
  

  
    03
    
    Generate UBL
    EN 16931 + CTC-FR
  

  
    04
    
    Validate
    XSD · Schematron · rules
  

  
    05
    
    Submit
    any Plateforme Agréée
  

  
    06
    
    Track
    lifecycle · disputes · payments
  

  
    07
    
    Operate
    set status · resend · email · credit note
  

| Step | What NomaUBL does |
|---|---|
| **Extract** | Pulls source documents from JDE BIP Print Queue, JDE archive directories, FTP/SFTP servers or local file system. Polls automatically or on demand. |
| **Transform** | Applies XSLT pre-processing, converts BI Publisher RTF templates to XSL, and bursts multi-document spools by configurable burst keys. |
| **Generate UBL** | Produces structured UBL 2.1 documents using template-aware defaults: parties, scheme IDs, BAR routing, business-process types, allowance/charge categories, French legal mentions. |
| **Validate** | Runs XSD + Schematron + the French CTC extension before any document leaves your perimeter. Surfaces every error, warning and recovery hint inline. |
| **Submit** | Sends to the configured Plateforme Agréée through a pluggable connector. The PA backend is configuration — swap it without code changes. |
| **Track** | Polls the PA for status updates and persists the full lifecycle: submitted, received, paid, disputed, refused, rejected — with reasons, expected actions, and timestamps. |
| **Operate** | Surfaces the right action at the right step: resend, email PDF to customer, mark payment received, issue credit note, set status, cancel accounting — driven by configurable API connectors. |

---

## One platform, every source system

NomaUBL is built around a **template model**: each source produces XML, NomaUBL maps it through templates, and every other module operates on the resulting UBL — regardless of which ERP fed it. Adding a new source is a configuration task, not a re-architecture.

    The PA backend is a configuration. Submit, retrieve lifecycle statuses, persist disputes, refusals, payment notifications. Switch your Plateforme Agréée without rebuilding the rest of your stack.
    Import · Retrieve Statuses
  

  
    
    Operate the lifecycle
    Resend, set status, email PDF, mark payment received, issue a credit note, cancel accounting — the right action surfaces at the right step. Every event is logged, append-only, audit-ready.
    E-Invoicing · Integration Errors
  

  
    
    Govern with self-service config
    Reference lists, document types, suppliers, BAR routing, payment codes, VAT categories, currency mappings — all maintained from the UI. Finance owns the rules, IT owns the platform.
    Configuration · File Versions

## NomaUBL vs the alternatives

A Plateforme Agréée is required by the regulation — but it is not the whole solution. The choices below show why NomaUBL is the natural complement.

The right pairing is **NomaUBL + a Plateforme Agréée** — not one or the other. NomaUBL takes care of everything *upstream* of the PA and *around* the PA; the PA handles the regulated transmission rail. Together, they cover the regulation end to end.

# === AI assistants ===

## Liberty Next — AI assistant
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/ai-assistant/

The Liberty Next AI assistant: the drawer opened from the AI Assistant button, what it can do (read the connectors' queries, call API endpoints, propose configuration, read allowed web pages), how it is restricted (ai:chat, allowed connectors, read-only queries, data scope), and its settings.

**AI Assistant**, at the right of the top bar, opens a drawer where users ask questions about their data in plain language. The assistant answers by running the connectors' queries, with the user's rights.

---

## At a glance

---

## Using it \{#use\}

Type a question and press Enter (Shift+Enter for a new line). The answer arrives as it is written, with the tools the assistant used; **Stop** interrupts it and keeps what was received; **new conversation** starts over. The conversation lives in the drawer: it is not kept after the page is reloaded.

Examples: *How many open orders per company this month?* — *Which users have not signed in since June?* — *Show the five largest invoices of ACME.*

---

## What it can do \{#tools\}

| Tool | Does | Setting |
|---|---|---|
| `list_connectors` | Lists the connectors, their queries and endpoints (descriptions, no SQL, no credentials). | **Connector tools** (on by default). |
| `sql_query` | Runs a **read** query of a SQL connector. Write queries are always refused. | **Connector tools**. |
| `api_call` | Calls an endpoint of an API connector. | **API tool** (off by default — an endpoint may change data). |
| Scaffold tools | Propose a query, a dictionary entry, a screen or a menu item; the user reviews the proposal and applies it. | **Scaffold tools** (off by default). |
| Web fetch | Reads pages of the allowed domains. | **Allowed domains** (none by default). |

The assistant only uses existing named queries: it does not write SQL against the database.

---

## Who can use it, and on what \{#access\}

- The user needs the `ai:chat` permission (a role's *AI assistant* rule, in **Beyond the menus**).
- **Allowed connectors** in Settings → App limits the connectors the assistant may reach; empty means all.
- Every query it runs goes through the same server checks as a screen: the user's [data scope](./build/secure/roles-and-permissions.md#data-scope) filters the rows.

---

## Settings \{#settings\}

In **Settings → App → AI Assistant**: **Enabled**, **Anthropic API key** (encrypted), **Model**, **Effort**, **Max tokens**, **Max tool iterations** (8), **Request timeout (s)**, **Adaptive thinking**, **System prompt**, the tools above and **Allowed connectors**. See [App settings](./build/settings-app.md#ai). Without a key, the drawer says the assistant is not configured.

---

## Tips \{#tips\}

- Give queries a clear label and description (Settings → Connectors): the assistant chooses its queries from them.
- Write dedicated read queries for the questions users ask often (totals per company, per month), rather than expecting the assistant to aggregate thousands of rows.
- Keep **API tool** off unless the endpoints are read-only.

---

## Liberty Next — Expose data to the AI assistant
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/cookbook/expose-to-ai/

Recipe — choose what the AI assistant reaches and help it pick the right query: the ai:chat permission, the allowed connectors, read queries only, the user's data scope, and query labels and descriptions written for the model.

## The problem

The [AI assistant](../ai-assistant.md) answers questions by running the connectors' named queries. It must reach the right data — and only that — and pick the right query for each question.

## The pattern

| Layer | Setting | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Who** | The `ai:chat` permission, through a role. | Without it, the user has no assistant. |
| **Which connectors** | **Allowed connectors**, Settings → App → AI Assistant. | Empty: every connector; otherwise only those listed. |
| **Which queries** | Read queries only. | Write queries are always refused; the assistant never writes SQL of its own. |
| **Which rows** | The user's rights and [data scope](../build/secure/roles-and-permissions.md#data-scope). | A query run by the assistant is checked like a screen's: the user sees the same rows. |
| **Which query to pick** | The queries' **label** and **description**. | The assistant reads them to choose. |

## The recipe

### 1. Grant the assistant

In **Settings → Access → Roles**, give the users' role the *AI assistant* rule (`ai:chat`), in **Beyond the menus**. See [Roles & permissions](../build/secure/roles-and-permissions.md).

### 2. Limit the connectors

In **Settings → App → AI Assistant**, fill **Allowed connectors** with the connectors whose data the assistant may read — for example the CRM's, without the HR one. Keep **API tool** off unless the endpoints only read.

### 3. Describe the queries

In **Settings → Connectors**, give each query the assistant should use a **label** and a **description** (Advanced tab). The assistant lists the connectors with their queries and descriptions, then picks one:

| Good | Weak |
|---|---|
| `Invoices of a period with customer, amount and status. For questions about invoicing volume, recent invoices, status breakdown.` | `Get invoices` |
| `Number of deals per pipeline stage. For pipeline breakdown questions.` | `Aggregate deals` |
| `Customer activities (calls, meetings, e-mails), most recent first. Parameter CUSTOMER_ID.` | `Activities` |

Two sentences are enough: **what the rows are**, and **which questions it answers**. Mention the parameters and their format.

### 4. Add dedicated queries

For the questions asked often — totals per company, per month — write a read query that computes them, rather than letting the assistant go through thousands of rows. Name its parameters clearly (`PERIOD_FROM`, `COMPANY`) and declare their labels.

### 5. Check

Sign in as a user of the role and ask a question the role should answer, then one it should not: the assistant shows the tools it used and the queries it ran.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Symptom |
|---|---|
| Queries without description | The assistant hesitates between similar queries, or picks the wrong one. |
| Several queries with the same description | Same. Make each description specific. |
| A sensitive connector left in an empty **Allowed connectors** list | The assistant may read it for any user who has rights on its queries. List the connectors explicitly. |
| Expecting the assistant to update data | Write queries are refused; changes go through screens and actions. |

## What's next

- [AI assistant](../ai-assistant.md) — the drawer, the tools, the settings.
- [Roles & permissions](../build/secure/roles-and-permissions.md) — `ai:chat` and the data scope.
- [App settings → AI Assistant](../build/settings-app.md#ai) — every setting.

---

## NomaUBL — AI Capabilities
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/nomaubl/application/ai-capabilities/

The NomaUBL AI assistant — a chat panel that knows the page and the invoice you are on, answers from the NomaUBL documentation, from the generated documentation of the instance and from its data (invoice dossier, period figures, backlog, lifecycle, validation errors, server log, integrity checks, e-directory), follows diagnostic playbooks, proposes follow-ups, and only reads.

The **AI Assistant** is a chat panel embedded in NomaUBL. It answers three kinds of questions:

- *How does the product work?* — from the NomaUBL documentation, indexed by the server, with the title and the link of the page it used.
- *How is this instance set up?* — from the [implementation report](reports/implementation-report.md) generated from the configuration of the instance: documents, mappings, rules, jobs, roles.
- *What is the state of my data?* — from the database, in **read-only** mode: one invoice in full, the figures of a period, the backlog, the errors, the server log, the integrity checks.

The assistant knows **the page you are on and the invoice you have open**, so *"why is this invoice refused?"* needs no number typed by hand. Replies stream as the model writes them; every tool call appears as a pill with the filters used; each reply ends with **follow-up buttons**. The assistant works in French or English and follows the language of the question.

---

## Opening the assistant

- Click **✦ AI Assistant** at the right end of the top bar. The panel opens as a drawer beside the page; it stays usable while an invoice window is open.
- Press **Enter** to send, **Shift+Enter** for a new line, **■** to stop a reply in progress.
- **The conversation is kept** when the panel is closed or the page reloaded (the last 40 messages, in the browser). **+ New chat** starts a fresh one.
- **Opening another invoice starts a new conversation**: the previous exchange was about another invoice and would mislead the model.

---

## At a glance

| Element | Role |
|---|---|
| **Model picker** | *Default* uses the model set by the administrator; the list offers Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Haiku 4.5. The choice is remembered in the browser. |
| **+ New chat** | Clears the conversation. |
| **Context bar** | The page you are on and, when an invoice window is open, a chip with the invoice number and status. **×** on the chip leaves the invoice out of the current chat. |
| **Tool pills** | Each tool called, with the filters it received. |
| **📋 Copy** | Copies the reply as Markdown, without the follow-up line. |
| **Domains and questions** | Above the input: the follow-ups of the last reply, or the four questions of a domain — see [Context and starter questions](#context-and-starter-questions). |

---

## Context and starter questions

With every question the panel sends the **current page**, its **navigation filter** and the **open invoice** (document, type, company, number, status, customer). The assistant assumes the question is about them unless told otherwise.

Above the input, a **domain picker** offers four questions per domain. A question ending with *…* only fills the input, to be completed (an invoice number, a customer).

| Domain | Questions |
|---|---|
| **This invoice** *(when an invoice is open)* | *Why is this invoice in this status?* · *Summarise its lifecycle* · *What should I fix to resubmit it?* · *What are its validation errors?* |
| **Period** | *Give me this month's invoice summary* · *Last month's summary, compared to the month before* · *Deposit rate and error rate this month* · *Net amounts deposited this month, per company* |
| **Backlog** | *Which invoices await an action and what to do?* · *Which refused invoices still await an action?* · *Any invoices pending at the platform for more than 2 days?* · *Which invoices are deposited but not transmitted?* |
| **Invoices** | *Which invoices failed this week and why?* · *Find invoice number …* · *Invoices of customer …* · *Any duplicates this month?* |
| **Statuses & errors** | *What does status 9906 mean?* · *What to do with an invoice refused by the customer?* · *What to do with an invoice rejected by the platform?* · *What does rule BR-FR-…* |
| **Configuration** | *Which documents are sent to the platform?* · *Which notification rules are active?* · *Who has access to what (roles and users)?* · *How is the platform connection configured?* |
| **Documentation** | *How do watched folders work?* · *How does e-reporting work?* · *How do I resend or reprocess an invoice?* · *What changed in the last release?* |
| **Technical** | *Any errors in the server log today?* · *Is the instance healthy?* · *Did all scheduled jobs run?* · *Run this month's integrity checks* |

The page chooses the starting domain: **This invoice** when an invoice is open; **Technical** on the IT dashboard, Diagnostics and Scheduled jobs; **Configuration** on Settings, Roles, Users, Developer, Documents, Notification rules, Actions and Watched folders; **Documentation** on the reference pages and the release notes; **Period** everywhere else — accounting and sales land on the period, IT on the instance.

Every reply ends with **one to three follow-ups** — the natural answer to a question the assistant asked, the next check, or a deeper question. They show in place of the domain's questions; a click on a domain brings its questions back.

---

## What the assistant uses

### Documentation

| Tool | Pill | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **`search_docs`** | 📚 | Searches the NomaUBL documentation, indexed by the server from the site's full-text export (`llms-full.txt`); returns the best pages with title, URL and passage. Called first for any product question. |
| **`read_doc_page`** | 📖 | Reads one page found by `search_docs`, in windows of 12,000 characters for long pages. |
| **`list_doc_pages`** | 📑 | The table of contents of the documentation, when the search finds nothing relevant. |
| **`instance_docs`** | 📘 | The [implementation report](reports/implementation-report.md) of this instance: table of contents, one section, or a search across sections. Called first for any question about how *this* instance is configured. |

The documentation is indexed per language: a French interface searches the French pages, an English interface the English ones. The index is refreshed every six hours; when the site cannot be reached, the assistant uses the copy of the documentation bundled with the application and says so in its answer.

The assistant quotes the page it used and gives its link. It never invents a setting, a status code or a URL: when the documentation does not cover a point, it says so.

### Data of the instance

| Tool | Pill | What it returns |
|---|---|---|
| **`invoice_dossier`** | 🧾 | Everything about one invoice in one call: header (status, customer, amounts, dates, PA identifier), lines, VAT breakdown, validation errors and the full lifecycle with the PA reasons. |
| **`list_invoices`** | 🧾 | Up to 50 invoices filtered on status, company, transaction type (B2B / B2BINT / B2C / B2G / OUTOFSCOPE), customer, invoice number (BT-1) and issue dates. |
| **`lifecycle_history`** | 🕘 | Every status event of an invoice, with the PA rejection reason, expected action and status note. |
| **`validation_errors`** | ⚠️ | The validation errors of an invoice (level, source, rule, message), as in [Integration errors](./diagnostics/integration-errors.md). |
| **`period_figures`** | 🗓️ | The summary of a period from the [audit report](reports/audit-report.md): indicators with the previous period and the variation, the breakdown of processed invoices, the findings, and the backlog across all periods (by status, company and age). Default: the current month to date. |
| **`billing_overview`** | 💶 | The figures of the [Billing overview](./billing-overview.md) for a period, sales or purchases: revenue excl. VAT with invoices and credit notes apart, VAT, counts, transmission or acceptance rate, compared with the previous period; twelve months by outcome; what needs a decision, all dates, in amounts; the split per company and per transaction type. Options: date basis (document date by default) and whether to count the reviewed errors. |
| **`status_statistics`** | 📈 | The data of the [Statistics](./statistics.md) dashboard for a period, sales or purchases: invoices by stage, status, activity code, reason and transaction type (count and amount), the same for the previous period, the trend per day, and the open invoices by waiting time. Same options. |
| **`dashboard_overview`** | 📊 | The counters of the [Operations](./dashboard.md) dashboard for a date range. |
| **`tech_dashboard`** | 🩺 | The health of the instance, as on the [IT dashboard](./tech-dashboard.md): JVM, scheduled jobs and their last runs, send failures, waiting invoices, configuration issues, table sizes. |
| **`server_log`** | 📜 | The end of the [server log](./diagnostics/server-log.md), newest first, filtered on level, module and text. |
| **`integrity_checks`** | 🔎 | The configured [integrity checks](../configuration/system/integrity-reports.md) and, for one check, its result on a date range. |
| **`list_ereports`** | 🔍 | Up to 50 e-reporting runs filtered on direction (inbound / outbound — each run carries both flows 10.1 and 10.3), company and status. |
| **`explain_status_code`** | 🏷️ | The tag and the FR / EN labels of an invoice or e-reporting status code. |
| **`reason_codes`** | 📋 | The PA rejection reasons and expected actions with their labels. |
| **`edirectory_lookup`** | 🏢 | A company in the [e-directory](./edirectory.md) by SIREN, SIRET or name: legal data and routing lines. |
| **`template_settings`** | ⚙️ | The settings of one template, secrets masked. Requires the *Settings access* feature. |

The assistant knows every page of the application — among them the [Billing overview](./billing-overview.md), [Statistics](./statistics.md), the [Explorer](./explorer.md) and the [invoice stages](./invoices.md#status-by-stage) — and answers a question on revenue, credit notes, transmission rate or decisions with `billing_overview`, a question on stages, waiting time or reasons with `status_statistics`. Through the implementation report (`instance_docs`) it also knows the default periods and the dashboard rules of the instance. The two tools answer only when the user's role grants the page (Billing overview, Statistics).

The assistant also receives the live **status catalogue**, so *"en litige"*, *"refused"* or *"awaiting deposit"* map to the right code.

The data tools follow the rights of the signed-in user: the company visibility of the role applies to the invoices, figures and backlog the assistant reads.

### Playbooks

For a diagnosis, the assistant first loads the matching **playbook** (🧭 `load_playbook`), then follows its steps. The built-in playbooks are:

| Playbook | Diagnosis |
|---|---|
| `refused-invoice` | An invoice awaiting an action (213, 9905, 9907, 9904, 207, 208, 210, 221, 206): what was refused, what to correct, how to resubmit — or, for a refusal, the internal credit note to issue. |
| `backlog` | What still awaits an action, for one company or all: to fix and resend, answer to the buyer expected, pending at the platform, deposited but not transmitted. |
| `missing-invoice` | An invoice or a JDE print job that did not reach NomaUBL: which step failed and what to run. |
| `ereporting-error` | A failed e-reporting run (9956 to 9959): the offending data and the correction. |
| `status-not-updated` | An invoice that keeps an old status although the platform moved on. |

The administrator can add playbooks or replace a built-in one under the same name, from the *Custom playbooks* field of the [global settings](../configuration/system/global.md) (*AI* tab).

At most **10 tool calls** are chained for one question. When a tool fails, the assistant gives the tool, the input and the error.

---

## Conversation examples

### Diagnosing the open invoice

> **User** — *(invoice F2026-1203 open)* Why is this invoice in this status?
>
> 🧭 `load_playbook · refused-invoice` &nbsp; 🧾 `invoice_dossier · 1203 RI 00001`
>
> **AI Assistant** — Invoice **F2026-1203** was **refused by the buyer** (status 210) on 2026-10-22 with the reason `PU_ERR` — incorrect unit prices. A refusal requires an internal credit note: cancel the invoice with a credit note, then issue a corrected invoice.
>
> *Follow-ups:* `Show its lifecycle` · `Other refusals this month?`

### Summary of the month

> **User** — Give me this month's invoice summary
>
> 🔍 `period_figures · 2026-10-01 → 2026-10-24`
>
> **AI Assistant** — 1,240 invoices processed (+6 % on September), 1,180 deposited — deposit rate 95 %. 38 await an action: 22 to fix and resend, 16 awaiting an answer to the buyer. First-pass validation: 97 %.
>
> | Awaiting | Count | Oldest |
> |---|---|---|
> | 9905 — Validation failed | 14 | 6 days |
> | 213 — Rejected | 8 | 3 days |
> | 210 — Refused | 16 | 9 days |
>
> *Follow-ups:* `Detail the 9905 errors` · `Which companies are behind?`

### How the product works

> **User** — How do watched folders work?
>
> 📚 `search_docs · watched folders` &nbsp; 📖 `read_doc_page · …/management/watched-folders`
>
> **AI Assistant** — A watched folder is scanned on a schedule; each new file is processed with the document it is bound to… *(Source: Watched Folders — link)*

---

## What the assistant cannot do

- **Change anything.** It only reads. Asked to resend, reprocess or change a setting, it says where in the application to do it.
- **Go beyond your rights.** The data tools apply the company visibility of your role, and the settings require the *Settings access* feature.
- **Read files.** The chat is text-only; a short XML pasted in the question is read, a file cannot be attached.

The administrator sets the API key, the default model, the documentation source, the custom playbooks, the system prompt and the tools from the *AI* tab of the [global settings](../configuration/system/global.md).

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Open the invoice, then ask.** The context chip gives the assistant the invoice; there is nothing to type. Use **×** on the chip to ask a general question without leaving the window.
- **Ask for a period summary in plain words.** *"This month"*, *"last quarter"*, *"our deposit rate"* — the assistant reads the figures of the audit report.
- **Click the follow-ups.** They carry on the diagnosis with the right next check.
- **Start a new chat for a new subject.** A long thread on another topic weighs on the answers.
- **Pick a heavier model for a long diagnosis**, the default for everyday questions.
- **Treat the panel as an external service.** Questions and tool results are sent to the model provider; avoid pasting personal data that the screens do not already show.
- **For exhaustive lists, use the dedicated pages.** The assistant characterises a problem; the [E-Invoicing](./invoices.md) list, [Diagnostics](./diagnostics/overview.md) and [Reports](reports/overview.md) give the full picture.

# === Liberty Next — framework ===

## Liberty Next — First app walkthrough
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/getting-started/first-app/

Build a working Liberty Next app end to end: a pool, a SQL connector with its queries generated from a table, a screen with a grid and an edit dialog, and a menu entry — all from Settings, applied without a restart.

This page goes from an empty install to a working app — a sidebar entry that opens a grid on a table, with an edit dialog. Everything is done from **Settings** (superuser), nothing is edited by hand.

Four elements, in order — **pool → connector → screen → menu** — each saved and applied at once.

---

## At a glance

The example uses the `default` pool and a small `tasks` table.

---

## Step 1 — The pool \{#pool\}

Open **Settings → Pools**. The installation created the `default` pool: on a Docker install it points at the bundled PostgreSQL database, on a Python install without PostgreSQL at a local SQLite file. It is enough for this walkthrough. To work on another database, add a pool with its URL — see [Connectors](../connectors.md#pools).

Create the example table with any SQL client connected to that database:

```sql
CREATE TABLE tasks (
  id        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  title     VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
  status    VARCHAR(10)  NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open',
  due_date  DATE
);
INSERT INTO tasks (id, title, status, due_date) VALUES
  (1, 'Draft sprint plan',      'open', '2026-06-10'),
  (2, 'Review pull request 42', 'done', '2026-06-05'),
  (3, 'Customer follow-up',     'open', '2026-06-12');
```

---

## Step 2 — The connector and its queries \{#connector\}

1. **Settings → Connectors → ＋ Connector**: name `tasks`, type **SQL**, pool `default`. Save.
2. With `tasks` selected, choose **Tables** in the mode bar, then **＋ Add queries → Generate from DB**.
3. In the CRUD wizard, pick the `tasks` table, keep every column, tick **key** on `ID`, and keep the four statements (SELECT, UPDATE, INSERT, DELETE).
4. Save. The connector now holds `tasks_get`, `tasks_put`, `tasks_post` and `tasks_delete`:

```sql
SELECT ID, TITLE, STATUS, DUE_DATE FROM tasks
UPDATE tasks SET TITLE = :TITLE, STATUS = :STATUS, DUE_DATE = :DUE_DATE WHERE ID = :ID_ORIGINAL
```

The columns are read from the database when the query runs; nothing else needs declaring. See [Create from a database table](../build/queries/create-from-database.md).

---

## Step 3 — The screen \{#screen\}

1. **Settings → Screens → ＋ Add scope**, pick `tasks`: the `tasks` chip appears.
2. **＋ Add screen**, id `tasks`. Click the new card to open the screen editor.
3. **General** tab: label `Tasks`; check **Editable** for in-grid editing.
4. **Queries** tab: read `tasks_get`, update `tasks_put`, insert `tasks_post`, delete `tasks_delete`.
5. **Dialog** tab: drag the columns onto the form.
6. **Save**.

The grid columns come from the read query; their labels and formats from the [dictionary](../dictionary.md) when entries exist (its **Scan a table** button proposes them). The [Screen Creation Assistant](../build/screen-assistant.md) does steps 2 and 3 in one pass for a table.

---

## Step 4 — The menu entry \{#menu\}

1. **Settings → Menus → + Add scope**, pick `tasks`: the empty tree of the app appears.
2. **＋ Item**, then in the inspector: label `Tasks`, type `screen`, target `tasks_get` (the screen built on it), icon `table`.
3. Save.

Since `tasks` now has a menu, it is an app: it appears in the app picker, and its sidebar shows **Tasks**. A click opens the grid: a row opens the edit dialog, **＋ Add** an empty one. See [Build the tree](../build/menus/build-the-tree.md) and [Make a connector an app](../build/menus/make-connector-an-app.md).

---

## What you have now

- **A pool** — the database connection.
- **A connector** — the four queries on the table.
- **A screen** — the grid and the dialog on these queries.
- **A menu** — the entry that opens the screen, which makes the connector an app.

Every save was applied without a restart. The pool and the connector are stored in `connectors.toml`, the screen in `screens.toml`, the menu in `menus.toml`.

---

- [Project layout](./project-layout.md) — where these files live.
- [Dictionary](../dictionary.md) — labels, lists of values and formats.
- [Roles & permissions](../build/secure/roles-and-permissions.md) — who may open the new screen.
- [CRM tutorial](../tutorial-crm/01-setup.md) — a complete app with several screens, a dashboard and jobs.

## Liberty Next — Project layout
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/getting-started/project-layout/

File map of the two repositories — liberty-next (framework binary) and liberty-apps (per-installation configuration). What lives where, what is committed, what is per-installation, and how LIBERTY_APPS_DIR routes the framework to the apps repo.

The Liberty Framework is split between **two repositories** that work together at runtime: the framework binary (`liberty-next`) reads its per-section configuration from the apps repo (`liberty-apps`). This page is the file map — where each piece lives, what is committed, what is per-installation.

---

## At a glance

The framework is told where the apps repo lives via the `LIBERTY_APPS_DIR` environment variable. Out of the box, with `LIBERTY_APPS_DIR` unset, the framework reads its per-section TOML from `liberty-next/config/` — convenient for local experimentation but not the production layout.

---

## `liberty-next` — the framework binary

```text
liberty-next/
├── start.sh                  ← run/dev helper (build, init-db, init-config, …)
├── pyproject.toml            ← Python deps + CLI entry points
├── liberty/                  ← FastAPI backend (Python 3.12)
│   ├── main.py               ← app factory, lifespan, routers
│   ├── config.py             ← TOML loading + env expansion
│   ├── connectors/           ← SQL / API connector engine, dictionary (dictionary.py)
│   ├── auth/                 ← local users, OIDC, JWT, permissions
│   ├── screens/              ← screen engine (grid + dialog runtime)
│   ├── dashboards/           ← dashboard layout + widget rendering
│   ├── charts/               ← chart definitions
│   ├── menus/                ← menu tree + permission pruning
│   ├── jobs/                 ← Nomaflow (jobs, steps, scheduler)
│   ├── actions/              ← shared actions
│   ├── notify/               ← notifications
│   ├── ai/                   ← Anthropic tool-use assistant
│   ├── licensing/            ← RS256 license-key verification
│   ├── web/                  ← HTTP routes (one module per area)
│   └── *_cli.py              ← CLI entry points (admin, connectors, crypto, license)
│
├── frontend/                 ← React 19 + Vite SPA (built to frontend/dist/)
│   └── src/
│       ├── pages/            ← pages, including Settings/ (one editor per configuration type)
│       ├── common/           ← shared UI parts (fields, lists, dialogs, SQL editor…)
│       ├── components/       ← layout (sidebar, app picker, tabs)
│       ├── locales/          ← interface texts, en and fr
│       └── api/              ← REST client
│
├── config/                   ← bundled templates + per-installation files
│   ├── app.toml              ← application settings — edited in Settings → App
│   ├── auth.toml             ← local users — created by init-db, gitignored
│   ├── *.toml.example        ← templates for connectors / dictionary / menus / screens / charts / dashboards
│   └── *.toml                ← real per-section files (only when LIBERTY_APPS_DIR is unset)
│
├── tests/                    ← pytest suite
└── docs/                     ← framework-internal planning notes (not the public docs)
```

| File | Status | Edited by |
|---|---|---|
| `liberty/`, `frontend/`, `pyproject.toml`, `start.sh` | Committed | Framework maintainers — *don't* edit per-installation. |
| `config/app.toml` | Per-installation | Settings → App. |
| `config/auth.toml` | Per-installation, gitignored | `liberty-admin` CLI / the Settings UI. |
| `config/*.toml.example` | Committed | Framework maintainers — bundled templates. |
| `config/*.toml` (without `.example`) | Per-installation, gitignored | Editable from the Settings UI when `LIBERTY_APPS_DIR` is unset. |

---

## `liberty-apps` — your configuration

```text
liberty-apps/
├── README.md
├── config/                   ← per-section TOML — read by liberty-next at runtime
│   ├── connectors.toml       ← pools, connectors and their queries / endpoints
│   ├── dictionary.toml       ← data items, enums, lookups, sequences
│   ├── menus.toml            ← one menu per app
│   ├── screens.toml          ← grids and dialogs
│   ├── charts.toml           ← saved charts
│   ├── dashboards.toml       ← dashboards
│   ├── actions.toml          ← shared actions
│   └── theme.toml            ← colours and branding
│
├── plugins/                  ← Python packages (functions called by steps and actions)
│   ├── <package>/            ← one folder per package, with __init__.py
│   └── nomaflow/
│       └── jobs.toml         ← the Nomaflow job catalogue
│
└── docs/                     ← deployment & operations notes (per-installation)
```

| File | Edited by | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `config/connectors.toml` | Settings UI → *Connectors* | Owns the pool registry plus every connector. |
| `config/dictionary.toml` | Settings UI → *Dictionary* | Per-column metadata reused by screens and charts. |
| `config/menus.toml` | Settings UI → *Menus* | One root per app, optional folder/leaf hierarchy. |
| `config/screens.toml` | Settings UI → *Screens* | Grids + dialogs + per-field conditions. |
| `config/dashboards.toml` | Settings UI → *Dashboards* | KPI, chart and table widgets. |
| `config/charts.toml` | Settings UI → *Charts* | Chart definitions referenced by dashboards. |
| `config/actions.toml` | Settings UI → *Actions* | Shared actions called by screens. |
| `config/theme.toml` | Settings UI → *Theme* | Colours and branding. |
| `plugins/nomaflow/jobs.toml` | Nomaflow → *Jobs* | The job catalogue. |
| `plugins/*/*.py` | Developer | Custom step callables — exposed to the framework via `sys.path`. |

Every file is plain TOML you can read with `cat`, diff with `git`, edit in `vim`. The Settings UI uses the same on-disk format — what you save in the browser is what `git status` reports.

---

## How the framework finds your config

The wiring is one environment variable:

```bash
export LIBERTY_APPS_DIR="$HOME/work/liberty-apps/config"
```

When `LIBERTY_APPS_DIR` is **set**:

| Config | Read from |
|---|---|
| `connectors.toml`, `dictionary.toml`, `menus.toml`, `screens.toml`, `charts.toml`, `dashboards.toml` | `${LIBERTY_APPS_DIR}/<name>.toml` |
| `app.toml` | `liberty-next/config/app.toml` *(stays per-host)* |
| `auth.toml` | `liberty-next/config/auth.toml` *(stays per-host)* |
| `plugins/` packages | `${LIBERTY_APPS_DIR}/../plugins/` added to `sys.path` |

When `LIBERTY_APPS_DIR` is **unset**, every file is read from `liberty-next/config/`. Convenient for a single-host dev install; in production keep them separate.

The full env-var contract is documented under [Configuration → Environment variables](../configuration/environment-variables.md).

---

## Naming conventions

- **App identifier** — every screen, menu and job carries an `app` field (e.g. `nomajde`, `nomasx1`, `tutorial`). It's the namespace for screen ids and the prefix of the sidebar entry.
- **Connector name** — short, kebab-case (`jdedwards`, `tasks`, `crm-sql`). The same name surfaces in the catalog page, the AI assistant tool list and the URL of a query.
- **Pool name** — short, lowercase. `default` is reserved for the framework's own pool.
- **Permission code** — `sql:<connector>:<query>` for SQL queries and `api:<connector>:<endpoint>` for HTTP/API endpoints. The Settings UI builds them automatically; no manual code is needed.

---

## Version control conventions

- `liberty-next` is upgraded by **switching git tags** — the framework binary is treated as an external dependency, not modified in place. The `liberty-apps` repo stays untouched across framework upgrades.
- `liberty-apps` is committed normally — every TOML edit done in the Settings UI ends up as a diff in the repo. Commits made by the operator are reviewable like any other code change.
- Secrets — JWT signing key, master key, license key, AI key — live in the **environment**, not in either repo. See [Encryption & secrets](../configuration/encryption-secrets.md).

---

## What's next

- [Configuration → Settings UI](../configuration/settings-ui.md) — the in-browser editor for everything under `liberty-apps/config/`.
- [Apps & Plugins → Apps](../apps/overview.md) — how to organise multiple apps inside `liberty-apps`.

## Liberty Next — Installation — overview
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/installation/overview/

How to install Liberty Next: pick Docker (light or full layout) or a Python install, run one command, sign in, add the licence and the licensed apps, switch on HTTPS. Every step afterwards — status, backup, upgrade, rollback — goes through the same command.

Liberty Next is one server — a web application, its API and its job scheduler in a single process — plus a database and a folder of configuration files. Installing it means choosing where that server runs; everything after that is done with **one command**: `./liberty` on a Docker host, `liberty-ops` on a Python install.

---

## At a glance

---

## Which installation? \{#choose\}

| You want… | Install | Page |
|---|---|---|
| A production or test server for several users | **Docker — full layout**: Liberty Next, PostgreSQL, Traefik (HTTPS), pgAdmin, Portainer on one host | [Docker](./docker.md#full) |
| A quick trial or a demo on a laptop | **Docker — light layout**: one container, SQLite | [Docker](./docker.md#light) |
| A host where Docker is not allowed | **Python install** with pipx, run by systemd, PostgreSQL of your own | [Python server](./python-server.md) |
| Several nodes in a Docker Swarm | **Swarm**: the full layout adapted to `docker stack deploy` | [Docker](./docker.md#swarm) |

The licensed applications (Nomasx-1, Nomajde) and the bundled Nomaflow jobs need PostgreSQL: choose the full layout or a Python install with your own PostgreSQL.

---

## Install in three commands \{#quickstart\}

On a Linux host with Docker and the Compose plugin:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/fblettner/liberty-next.git
cd liberty-next/release
./liberty install full          # or: ./liberty install light
```

The command generates the secrets, starts the stack, waits until it answers and prints the sign-in details. Open `http://<host>/` (port `8000` on the light layout), sign in as **`admin`** with the printed password, and the server is ready.

Then, in this order and only if you need them:

1. **Licence** — *Settings → App → License*: paste the key you were delivered.
2. **Licensed apps** — `./liberty apps liberty_apps-<version>-py3-none-any.whl` ([Licensed apps](./deploy-prebuilt-apps.md)).
3. **HTTPS** — `./liberty ssl letsencrypt --domain liberty.example.com --email ops@example.com` ([HTTPS and Traefik](./traefik.md)).

---

## The one command \{#one-command\}

Every operation on a Docker install goes through `release/liberty`, run from the `release/` folder:

| Command | Use it to |
|---|---|
| `./liberty install [light\|full]` | Install (once). |
| `./liberty status` | See versions, health, pending migrations, last upgrade. |
| `./liberty doctor` | List what is wrong and how to fix it. |
| `./liberty apps <wheel>` | Add or refresh the licensed apps. |
| `./liberty ssl letsencrypt\|provided\|off` | Switch HTTPS on, change mode or switch it off. |
| `./liberty backup` / `restore <dir>` | Save and restore everything the install holds. |
| `./liberty upgrade` / `rollback` | Upgrade with a backup first; undo the last upgrade. |

A Python install has the same verbs in `liberty-ops`. The full reference is on [Operations](./operations.md).

:::warning[Never run `docker compose -f …` by hand]
The install records which compose files it uses (layout, HTTPS, licensed apps) in `release/.env`. A `docker compose -f docker-compose.full.yml up -d` names only the first file: the container comes back without the licensed apps and without HTTPS, and the install looks empty. Use `./liberty start`, `./liberty upgrade`… which always reuse the recorded files.
:::
