## Liberty Next — Architecture
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/installation/architecture/

What a Liberty Next install is made of, whatever the way it is installed (Docker light, Docker full, Python with systemd): one server process, a framework database, configuration files, the optional licensed-apps bundle and two secrets — where each one lives, how the server starts, how its health is checked.

A Liberty Next install always has the same parts. Docker or Python only changes **where** each part lives and which command drives it (`./liberty` or `liberty-ops`).

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| **The server** | One Python process: the web application, the REST API, the Nomaflow job scheduler and the live updates (Socket.IO) on the same port. |
| **The framework database** | Nomaflow run history, saved grid views, change packages, notifications, upgrade history — and users and roles when they are kept in the database rather than in `auth.toml`. |
| **The configuration** | TOML files: pools, connectors, dictionary, menus, screens, dashboards, charts, notification rules, Nomaflow jobs, application settings. Everything saved in **Settings** is written there. |
| **The licensed apps** *(optional)* | Nomasx-1, Nomajde and their jobs: configuration files, Python code (`plugins/`) and reference data, delivered as one wheel. |
| **Two secrets** | The master key, which encrypts the passwords stored in the configuration, and the key that signs the sessions. |

The data the applications show stays in **your** databases (Oracle, PostgreSQL…): Liberty Next reads them through the pools of its configuration and copies nothing unless a Nomaflow job is told to.

---

## At a glance — the full Docker layout

---

## Three ways to run it \{#layouts\}

| | Docker — light | Docker — full | Python |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Server** | `liberty-next` container | `liberty-next` container | pipx package run by systemd |
| **Around it** | — | PostgreSQL 16, Traefik, pgAdmin, Portainer containers | Your PostgreSQL, your reverse proxy |
| **Framework database** | SQLite | Bundled PostgreSQL | Your PostgreSQL (SQLite for a trial) |
| **Address** | `http://<host>:8000/` | `http(s)://<host>/` | `http://<host>:8000/` behind your proxy |
| **HTTPS** | Your own proxy | Traefik ([HTTPS and Traefik](./traefik.md)) | Your own proxy |
| **Licensed apps** | Possible, but they need PostgreSQL | Yes | Yes |
| **Operations command** | `./liberty` | `./liberty` | `liberty-ops` |
| **Page** | [Docker](./docker.md#light) | [Docker](./docker.md#full) | [Python server](./python-server.md) |

On the full layout Traefik is the only entry point: it sends `/` to Liberty Next and `/pgadmin`, `/portainer`, `/traefik` to the tools. PostgreSQL is published on `127.0.0.1:5432` only — reachable from the host or through an SSH tunnel, not from the network.

---

## Where the configuration lives \{#configuration\}

The configuration is split in two places — the same rule for Docker and Python:

| Files | Location |
|---|---|
| `app.toml` (application settings, licence, AI, SSO, SMTP) and `auth.toml` (local users and roles) | The `config/` folder of the server's working directory — or the file named by `LIBERTY_APP_CONFIG` for `app.toml`. |
| `connectors.toml`, `dictionary.toml`, `menus.toml`, `screens.toml`, `dashboards.toml`, `charts.toml`, `notifications.toml`… | The folder named by **`LIBERTY_APPS_DIR`** when it is set — the `config/` folder of the licensed apps — otherwise the same `config/` folder. |
| `jobs.toml` (Nomaflow) | `plugins/nomaflow/jobs.toml` next to that folder (`LIBERTY_APPS_DIR/../plugins/…`), otherwise `config/jobs.toml`. |
| History of the configuration and of the upgrades (`.versions/`) | Next to `connectors.toml`. |

Hence the layout of the licensed apps folder, the same in Docker and in Python:

```text
apps/
├── config/      ← LIBERTY_APPS_DIR: connectors, screens, menus, dictionary… and .bundled/ (what was delivered)
├── plugins/     ← the apps' Python code, and nomaflow/jobs.toml
└── data/        ← reference data loaded at installation
```

---

## Where everything lives \{#volumes\}

| What | Docker — light | Docker — full | Python (paths of the [Python server](./python-server.md) page) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `app.toml`, `auth.toml` | volume `liberty-config` | volume `liberty-config` | `/var/lib/liberty-next/config/` |
| Other configuration files | volume `liberty-config`, or `release/apps/config/` with the licensed apps | same | `/var/lib/liberty-next/apps/config/` |
| Licensed apps code and data | `release/apps/plugins/`, `release/apps/data/` (mounted on `/apps`) | same | `/var/lib/liberty-next/apps/plugins/`, `…/data/` |
| Framework database | SQLite in volume `liberty-data` | PostgreSQL in volume `pg-data` | your PostgreSQL server |
| Licensed apps databases (`nomasx1`, `nomajde`) | — | PostgreSQL in `pg-data` | your PostgreSQL server |
| Secrets | `release/.env` | `release/.env` | `/etc/liberty/secrets.env` |
| Tools, certificates | — | volumes `pgadmin-data`, `portainer-data`, `traefik-acme` | — |
| Backups | `release/backups/` | `release/backups/` | `backups/` next to the configuration folder |

On Docker, stopping, recreating or upgrading the containers never touches the volumes nor `release/apps/`; only `docker compose down -v` or `./liberty install --reset` deletes the volumes. What each backup contains is on [Operations](./operations.md#backup).

---

## The two secrets \{#secrets\}

The Docker installation generates both into `release/.env` (mode `0600`); on a Python install you generate them into the service's environment file. Keep a copy outside the server.

| Secret | Used for | If it changes |
|---|---|---|
| `LIBERTY_MASTER_KEY` | Encrypts every `ENC:` value of the configuration: pool passwords, the licence key, the AI key, the OIDC secret, the SMTP password. | Every encrypted value becomes unreadable — the pools stop connecting. Never change it on an existing install. |
| `LIBERTY_JWT_SECRET` | Signs the session tokens. | Everybody is signed out and signs in again. Nothing else is lost. |

`doctor` (Docker or Python) checks that both are at least 32 characters long and that the master key really decrypts every pool password. Every `LIBERTY_*` and `POSTGRES_*` variable can also be read from a file: `LIBERTY_MASTER_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/master_key` (Docker, Swarm or Kubernetes secrets).

---

## What happens when the server starts \{#startup\}

1. The settings are read; `${VARIABLE}` references in the TOML files are replaced by the environment.
2. *Docker only:* secrets given as files are read, the ownership of the configuration volume and of the apps folder is fixed, then the process drops root and runs as the `liberty` user (uid 1000). On a first start without licensed apps, the default configuration files are copied into `liberty-config` — an existing file is never overwritten.
3. *Docker only:* `liberty-admin init-db` creates the framework tables that are missing and, on the very first start, the `admin` user. On a Python install you run it once yourself.
4. The framework's own tables are compared with the version of the code: a missing column is added and recorded in **Settings → History → Upgrades**.
5. Pending schema migrations of the licensed apps are reported in the log; they are applied by the upgrade or by `migrate` (Docker: also at start-up with `LIBERTY_AUTO_MIGRATE=1`).
6. The server starts answering, even if the framework database is still unreachable — so that a pool can be fixed from **Settings**. `/ready` says when the database answers.

---

## Health and versions \{#health\}

| URL | Answers | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| `/health` | The process is up. | Liveness probes. |
| `/ready` | The framework database answers (`503` when it does not). | The Docker healthcheck — a stack whose database is down shows **unhealthy** — and `liberty-ops start`, which waits for it. |
| `/info` | Version and counts; connector and pool names only for a signed-in user. | Quick checks, support. |
| `/docs`, `/redoc` | The REST API reference. | Developers — see [REST API](../references/rest-api.md). |

Versions, pending migrations and the last upgrade are gathered by `status` — see [Operations](./operations.md#status).

---

## Liberty Next — Docker
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/installation/docker/

Install Liberty Next with Docker: prerequisites, the light layout (one container, SQLite) and the full layout (PostgreSQL, Traefik, pgAdmin, Portainer), install options, image tags, the recorded compose files, Docker Swarm.

Docker is the recommended way to run Liberty Next. The public image is `ghcr.io/fblettner/liberty-next`; the `release/` folder of the repository holds the compose files and the `liberty` command that drives them. Nothing is built on the host.

For what the two layouts contain, see [Architecture](./architecture.md#layouts).

---

## At a glance

---

## Before you start \{#prerequisites\}

| Need | Detail |
|---|---|
| A Linux host | Any distribution that runs Docker Engine. A macOS or Windows machine with Docker Desktop is fine for a trial. |
| Docker Engine and the Compose plugin | `docker compose version` must answer (Compose v2). |
| `git` and `curl` | To fetch `release/` and, if needed, a wheel by URL. |
| Free ports | Full layout: `80` (and `443` for HTTPS). Light layout: `8000`. |
| Disk | About 2 GB free for the images; `./liberty doctor` warns below 2 GB. |
| Memory | The bundled PostgreSQL is tuned with `shared_buffers = 2GB`: give the full layout a host with several GB of memory. |

Fetch the release folder:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/fblettner/liberty-next.git
cd liberty-next/release
```

Every command on this page and on the following ones is run from this `release/` folder.

---

## Full layout \{#full\}

```bash
./liberty install full
```

The command:

1. checks Docker and Compose;
2. writes `release/.env` with random secrets (master key, JWT secret, PostgreSQL, pgAdmin and Traefik dashboard passwords) and the list of compose files in use;
3. pulls the images and starts the five containers;
4. waits until `liberty-next` reports **healthy**;
5. prints the addresses and the passwords.

```text title="End of the output (example)"
  Liberty:    http://liberty.example.com/
  ReDoc:      http://liberty.example.com/redoc
  pgAdmin:    http://liberty.example.com/pgadmin
  Portainer:  http://liberty.example.com/portainer

  Sign in to Liberty as:
    username:  admin
    password:  Xq7…

  pgAdmin:        admin@liberty.fr / …
  Traefik:        admin / …   (dashboard at …/traefik — shown once; ./liberty dashboard-password regenerates)
  Postgres:       published on 127.0.0.1:5432 only (POSTGRES_BIND=0.0.0.0 in .env to open it)
```

Write the passwords down: the Traefik dashboard password is shown only once (`.env` keeps only its hash). The Liberty and pgAdmin passwords stay in `.env`.

Open the Liberty address, sign in as **`admin`**, then go on with the [licence and the licensed apps](./deploy-prebuilt-apps.md) and [HTTPS](./traefik.md).

---

## Light layout \{#light\}

```bash
./liberty install light
```

One container, a SQLite database, port `8000`: open `http://<host>:8000/` and sign in as **`admin`** with the printed password. Change the port with `LIBERTY_PORT` in `.env`, then `./liberty restart`.

The light layout has no Traefik, so no HTTPS of its own: on a shared network, put it behind your own reverse proxy or use the full layout.

---

## Install options \{#options\}

`./liberty install` accepts the layout and these options; they can be combined.

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `light` / `full` | The layout. Without it, the command asks. |
| `--tag 7.0.58` | Pin a release instead of `latest` (see [Image tags](#tags)). |
| `--apps <wheel or URL>` | Install the licensed apps right after the stack is up — see [Licensed apps](./deploy-prebuilt-apps.md). |
| `--ssl letsencrypt --domain D --email E` | HTTPS with a Let's Encrypt certificate (full layout). |
| `--ssl provided --domain D --cert-dir DIR --cert-file F --key-file K` | HTTPS with your own certificate (full layout). |
| `--reset` | **Deletes** the stack, its volumes and `.env`, then stops. Run the install again afterwards. |

A production install in one line:

```bash
./liberty install full --tag 7.0.58 \
  --ssl letsencrypt --domain liberty.example.com --email ops@example.com \
  --apps ./liberty_apps-7.0.58-py3-none-any.whl
```

The licence key is not an option: paste it in **Settings → App → License** once signed in.

### Running the install again \{#rerun\}

Running `./liberty install` on a host that already has a `.env` is safe: the secrets, the volumes and the recorded compose files are kept, and the stack is started again if it was stopped. To change HTTPS or the apps afterwards, use `./liberty ssl …` and `./liberty apps …` rather than a new install.

If a previous install left volumes behind but its `.env` is gone, the install refuses to start: the old database was created with passwords nobody has any more. Restore the old `.env`, or wipe everything with `./liberty install --reset` and install again.

---

## Image tags \{#tags\}

| `LIBERTY_IMAGE_TAG` in `.env` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `latest` (default) | The most recent release. Each upgrade takes the newest one. |
| `7.0.58` | That release, until you choose another. Recommended in production. |

Change it with `./liberty upgrade --tag <version>`, which also takes a backup and applies the migrations — see [Upgrade and rollback](./upgrading.md).

---

## The recorded compose files \{#compose-file\}

The install writes in `.env` which compose files make up the stack — the layout, then the HTTPS file, then the licensed apps file:

```env title="release/.env (excerpt)"
COMPOSE_FILE=docker-compose.full.yml:docker-compose.tls-letsencrypt.yml:docker-compose.apps.yml
```

Only `./liberty ssl …` and `./liberty apps …` change this line; every other command reuses it as it is. Two consequences:

- Use `./liberty start`, `stop`, `restart`, `logs`, `upgrade` for day-to-day work.
- A plain `docker compose ps` or `docker compose logs` without `-f` is fine (Compose reads the same line). **Never** pass `-f docker-compose.full.yml`: Compose would then ignore the other files, recreate the container without the licensed apps and without HTTPS, and the install would look empty.

---

## Docker Swarm \{#swarm\}

`docker-compose.swarm.yml` is the full layout adapted to `docker stack deploy`: same five services, overlay network, every service placed on a manager node.

```bash
docker swarm init                     # once, on the manager
./install.sh prepare                  # writes .env only, starts nothing
./deploy-swarm.sh                     # deploys or updates the stack "liberty"
./deploy-swarm.sh --status            # state of the services
./deploy-swarm.sh --rm                # removes the stack (volumes are kept)
```

`docker stack deploy` does not read `.env`: `deploy-swarm.sh` loads it into the shell first, so the values are fixed when the stack is deployed. After a change in `.env`, run `./deploy-swarm.sh` again.

What differs from Compose:

- The `liberty` command, `--ssl` and `--apps` work with the Compose layouts only. On Swarm, add the HTTPS or apps settings to the stack file yourself.
- PostgreSQL must stay on one node so that its volume follows it: add `node.hostname == <node>` to its placement constraints on a multi-node swarm. Traefik must run on a manager.
- Keep one replica of `liberty-next`: live updates are held in the process, so several replicas would show users different states.
- Upgrade one service with `docker service update --image ghcr.io/fblettner/liberty-next:<version> liberty_liberty-next`, undo it with `docker service rollback liberty_liberty-next`.
- `backup.sh` works the same way (the volume names are identical); restore with the stack removed.

---

## Liberty Next — Python server
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/installation/python-server/

Install Liberty Next without Docker: pipx install from PyPI, secrets in an environment file, PostgreSQL bootstrap with liberty-admin init-db, the licensed apps, a systemd unit, and liberty-ops for status, backups and upgrades.

For hosts where Docker is not an option, Liberty Next installs from PyPI as a Python application. The web application is included in the package: there is nothing to build. You bring the PostgreSQL server; `liberty-ops` then does what `./liberty` does on Docker — status, checks, backups, upgrades.

---

## At a glance

---

## Before you start \{#prerequisites\}

| Need | Detail |
|---|---|
| Python 3.12 or later | `python3 --version`. |
| pipx | `apt install pipx` (Debian, Ubuntu), `brew install pipx` (macOS), or `python3 -m pip install --user pipx`; then `pipx ensurepath`. |
| PostgreSQL 13 or later | Needed for the licensed apps and the Nomaflow jobs. A local server, a managed service or an existing server — with a role allowed to create roles and databases. Without licensed apps, SQLite is enough for a trial. |
| The apps wheel *(licensed only)* | `liberty_apps-<version>-py3-none-any.whl`, same version as the framework. |
| systemd *(recommended)* | To run the server unattended; `liberty-ops start / stop / logs` drive it. |

---

## 1 — Install the package \{#install\}

```bash
pipx install 'liberty-next[all]'
```

On a server, install it as the service user created in [step 2](#secrets) — `sudo -u liberty pipx install 'liberty-next[all]'` — so that the systemd unit finds it in that user's home.

`[all]` adds the optional parts: PDF reports, the LDAP job step and the schema migrations of the licensed apps. pipx puts these commands on the `PATH`:

| Command | Use |
|---|---|
| `liberty-next` | Starts the server (web application and API on the same port). |
| `liberty-ops` | Operations: status, doctor, backup, restore, upgrade, rollback — see [Operations](./operations.md#liberty-ops). |
| `liberty-admin` | Database bootstrap, users and roles, schema migrations — see [CLI](../references/cli.md). |
| `liberty-license` | Checks a licence key. |
| `liberty-crypto` | Encrypts a value into an `ENC:` string. |

---

## 2 — Create the system user and the secrets \{#secrets\}

```bash
sudo useradd --system --create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin liberty
sudo install -d -m 0750 -o liberty -g liberty /etc/liberty /var/lib/liberty-next /var/lib/liberty-next/apps/config
openssl rand -base64 48 | tr -d '\n=+/'     # run twice: one value per secret
```

```bash title="/etc/liberty/secrets.env  (mode 0640, owner root:liberty)"
LIBERTY_MASTER_KEY=<first random value>
LIBERTY_JWT_SECRET=<second random value>

POSTGRES_USER=liberty
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=<password of the liberty role>
POSTGRES_HOST=db.example.com
POSTGRES_PORT=5432
POSTGRES_DB=liberty

LIBERTY_APPS_DIR=/var/lib/liberty-next/apps/config
```

| Variable | Role |
|---|---|
| `LIBERTY_MASTER_KEY` | Encrypts every `ENC:` value of the configuration. Generate it once and never change it — see [Architecture](./architecture.md#secrets). |
| `LIBERTY_JWT_SECRET` | Signs the sessions. At least 32 characters. |
| `POSTGRES_*` | Read once by `init-db` to write the `default` pool, with its password encrypted by the master key. |
| `LIBERTY_APPS_DIR` | The folder of the configuration files (connectors, screens, menus…). The licensed apps' code goes next to it, in `../plugins`. `app.toml` and `auth.toml` stay in `config/` under the working directory, `/var/lib/liberty-next` — see [Architecture](./architecture.md#configuration). |

Every command below runs **as the `liberty` user with this file loaded**:

```bash
sudo -u liberty bash -c 'set -a; . /etc/liberty/secrets.env; set +a; <command>'
```

---

## 3 — Prepare PostgreSQL \{#postgres\}

Once, with a PostgreSQL superuser:

```sql
CREATE ROLE liberty LOGIN PASSWORD '<password of the liberty role>' CREATEROLE CREATEDB;
CREATE DATABASE liberty OWNER liberty;
```

`CREATEROLE` and `CREATEDB` let the licensed apps' installation create their own roles and databases (`nomasx1`, `nomajde`).

Then create the framework tables and the first user:

```bash
liberty-admin init-db
```

`init-db` writes the `default` pool, creates the framework tables and the `admin` superuser, and prints its password once. Run again, it changes nothing. To choose the password yourself: `liberty-admin init-db --password-env ADMIN_PASSWORD`.

---

## 4 — Add the licensed apps *(licensed only)* \{#apps\}

```bash
pipx inject liberty-next ./liberty_apps-<version>-py3-none-any.whl
liberty-apps install --target "$LIBERTY_APPS_DIR"
liberty-admin run-install-jobs
```

1. `pipx inject` adds the apps package to the same environment as the framework.
2. `liberty-apps install` writes the configuration files into `$LIBERTY_APPS_DIR` and the Python code into `../plugins` next to it. On an existing folder it merges entity by entity and keeps your changes — see [Licensed apps](./deploy-prebuilt-apps.md#merge).
3. `run-install-jobs` runs the installation jobs in order: `deploy-databases` (application roles and databases, then the Nomasx-1 schema) and `nomasx1-import-reference` (reference data). A job already completed is skipped; `--force` runs everything again.

---

## 5 — Run under systemd \{#systemd\}

```ini title="/etc/systemd/system/liberty-next.service"
[Unit]
Description=Liberty Next
After=network-online.target postgresql.service
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=liberty
Group=liberty
WorkingDirectory=/var/lib/liberty-next
EnvironmentFile=/etc/liberty/secrets.env
ExecStart=/home/liberty/.local/bin/liberty-next
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
NoNewPrivileges=true
PrivateTmp=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/liberty-next

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

Adjust `ExecStart` to the path `which liberty-next` gives for the `liberty` user. Then:

```bash
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now liberty-next
liberty-ops status
```

`liberty-ops` drives the unit named `liberty-next`; set `LIBERTY_SERVICE` if yours has another name.

The server listens on `http://<host>:8000/` (the port of **Settings → App**). Sign in as **`admin`**, then paste the licence key in **Settings → App → License**. For HTTPS, put the reverse proxy of your choice in front and forward WebSocket traffic (`/socket.io`) as well.

---

## Day to day \{#day-to-day\}

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Health, versions, pending migrations | `liberty-ops status` |
| Find what is wrong | `liberty-ops doctor` |
| Start, stop, restart, follow the log | `liberty-ops start` · `stop` · `restart` · `logs -f` |
| Back up | `liberty-ops backup --keep 30` |
| Upgrade | `liberty-ops upgrade` — see [Upgrade and rollback](./upgrading.md#python) |
| New admin password | `liberty-admin set-password admin` (prints a random one) |

Run them as the `liberty` user with the secrets loaded, as in [step 2](#secrets). The full list is on [Operations](./operations.md#liberty-ops).

---

## Liberty Next — Licensed apps
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/installation/deploy-prebuilt-apps/

Install Nomasx-1 and Nomajde on Liberty Next: the licence key, the apps wheel, the application databases created by the installation jobs, the per-entity merge that keeps your changes on every upgrade, and the first connection to the source system.

Nomasx-1, Nomajde and their Nomaflow jobs are delivered as one Python wheel, `liberty_apps-<version>-py3-none-any.whl`, and unlocked by a licence key. The framework runs without them; adding them takes one command.

---

## 1 — The licence key \{#set-the-license-key\}

Sign in as a superuser and open **Settings → App → License**. Paste the key you were delivered and save: the key is encrypted with the install's master key and the licensed connectors appear at once, without a restart.

Without a key, the apps install but their licensed connectors stay hidden. `liberty-license status` (in the container: `docker exec -u liberty liberty-next liberty-license status`) shows what the key covers and when it expires — see [Licence key](../framework/build/secure/license-key.md).

---

## 2 — Install the apps \{#install\}

On a Docker install, from `release/`:

```bash
./liberty apps ./liberty_apps-7.0.58-py3-none-any.whl     # or an https:// URL
```

The command:

1. prints the **merge plan** — what will be added, refreshed, kept or removed in the configuration (see [below](#merge));
2. unpacks the wheel into `release/apps/` (`config/`, `plugins/`, `data/`) with the Liberty Next image already on the host — the host needs no Python;
3. adds the apps folder to the recorded compose files and restarts the stack; the folder is mounted on `/apps`, and what **Settings** saves for the apps is written there;
4. runs the **installation jobs** in order:
   - `deploy-databases` — creates the `nomasx1` and `nomajde` roles and databases on the bundled PostgreSQL, then the Nomasx-1 schema;
   - `nomasx1-import-reference` — loads the reference data (Segregation of Duties baseline, settings, lists);
5. applies the pending schema migrations.

To install the apps together with the stack: `./liberty install full --apps ./liberty_apps-….whl`.

On a Python install, the same steps are three commands — see [Python server](./python-server.md#apps).

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--dry-run` | Prints the merge plan and stops: nothing is written. |
| `--force-config` | Also refreshes the vendor entities you changed without marking them as yours (see below). |

---

## 3 — Connect the source system \{#source\}

The apps read their data from your source system through a pool. Open **Settings → Pools**, fill in the pool the apps expect (`jdedwards` for JD Edwards EnterpriseOne) with a read-only account, test it, then run the collection jobs from **Nomaflow**. The order and the parameters of these jobs are on [Nomaflow → Bundled jobs](../nomaflow/bundled-jobs.md).

---

## Upgrading the apps — your changes are kept \{#merge\}

A new wheel brings new screens, menu items, dictionary entries, queries and dashboards, while you may have changed some of the delivered ones. The installer compares three versions of every entity — what was delivered last time, what is on the server now, what the new wheel brings — and decides entity by entity:

| Entity | What happens |
|---|---|
| New in the wheel | Added. |
| Delivered, never changed on the server | Refreshed with the new version. |
| Changed on the server | **Kept**, and listed at the end for review. |
| Marked `override = true` (the *Override* switch of the entity's General tab) | Always kept. |
| Created on the server | Always kept. |
| Withdrawn by the vendor | Removed only if it was never changed. |
| Pools and every `ENC:` secret | Always taken from your configuration. |
| `theme.toml` | Always yours. |

What was delivered is recorded under `config/.bundled/`, so the next upgrade knows "never changed" from "changed". The entities kept because they were changed locally are listed at the end of the run: mark them `override = true` to keep them for good, or install again with `--force-config` to take the vendor version.

The apps upgrade together with the framework with `./liberty upgrade --apps <wheel>` — see [Upgrade and rollback](./upgrading.md#apps).

---

## Check the installation \{#verify\}

| Check | Where |
|---|---|
| Apps version | `./liberty status` → `apps bundle` |
| Licence | **Settings → App → License** |
| Apps in the switcher | Nomasx-1 and Nomajde appear at the top of the sidebar |
| Installation jobs | The Nomaflow run history: `deploy-databases` and `nomasx1-import-reference` succeeded |
| Schema up to date | `./liberty status` → `migrations: up to date` |

---

## A second Nomasx-1 side by side \{#second-instance\}

To analyse two source systems separately on one server, the `nomasx1-init-db` job clones the Nomasx-1 configuration under a new name (for example `nomasx1b`) with its own database. See [Bundled jobs → nomasx1-init-db](../nomaflow/bundled-jobs.md#nomasx1-init-db).

---

## Wheel or packages? \{#packages\}

| Channel | Carries | Owned by |
|---|---|---|
| The apps wheel (this page) | The whole product: every configuration file, the Python code, the reference data. | The vendor — one per release. |
| The **Packages** screen | A selection of screens, menu items or dashboards with what they depend on. | You — to move your own changes from test to production. See [Packages](../framework/build/packages.md). |

Both use the same per-entity merge, so a wheel upgrade and a package import never overwrite each other's changes.

---

## Common problems \{#pitfalls\}

| Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|
| The licensed apps are missing from the switcher | Check the licence in **Settings → App → License**; `./liberty doctor` checks that the apps folder is in the recorded compose files. |
| After a manual `docker compose -f … up -d` the install looks empty | The apps folder was left out. Run `./liberty apps <wheel>` again (it changes nothing else) — then keep to `./liberty` commands. |
| `deploy-databases` fails with *permission denied* | The `default` pool needs a role allowed to create roles and databases. On the full layout it is the bundled `liberty` superuser. |
| A new vendor screen did not appear | It was kept because you changed it locally: see the list printed at the end, or install again with `--force-config`. |
| The wheel URL cannot be downloaded | Download it first and pass the local file. |

---

## Liberty Next — HTTPS and Traefik
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/installation/traefik/

Switch Liberty Next to HTTPS on the full Docker layout: a Let's Encrypt certificate or your own, switching mode or back to HTTP with ./liberty ssl, the Traefik dashboard password, and what to forward when you use your own reverse proxy.

On the full layout, Traefik receives every request and forwards it: `/` to Liberty Next, `/pgadmin`, `/portainer`, `/traefik` to the tools. It is also where HTTPS is switched on. One command does it, at any time after the installation.

---

## At a glance

---

## Let's Encrypt \{#letsencrypt\}

For a server reachable from the internet:

```bash
./liberty ssl letsencrypt --domain liberty.example.com --email ops@example.com
```

| Requirement | Why |
|---|---|
| The name resolves to this host (DNS A or AAAA record). | Let's Encrypt checks the name before issuing. |
| Ports `80` and `443` are reachable from the internet. | The certificate is obtained through a TLS challenge on `443`. |

Traefik requests the certificate on the first HTTPS call and renews it on its own. Certificates are kept in the `traefik-acme` volume, which no reset deletes (Let's Encrypt limits how often a certificate can be issued for the same name).

---

## Your own certificate \{#provided\}

For an internal server, a company certificate authority or a host without internet access:

```bash
./liberty ssl provided --domain liberty.internal.example.com \
  --cert-dir /etc/pki/liberty --cert-file liberty.crt --key-file liberty.key
```

The certificate folder is mounted read-only into Traefik and `traefik/dynamic/tls.yml` is generated with the two file names. To renew, replace the two files in the folder, then restart Traefik (`docker compose restart traefik` from `release/`). To add certificates for other names, edit `tls.yml`: Traefik reloads it on its own.

---

## What HTTPS changes \{#effects\}

- Liberty Next, pgAdmin and Portainer answer on `https://<domain>/…`; plain HTTP calls are redirected to HTTPS.
- Liberty Next responses carry security headers (no framing by other sites, no content-type guessing, a strict referrer policy).
- The routes answer only for the declared domain name.

---

## Change mode or go back to HTTP \{#switch\}

```bash
./liberty ssl provided …        # from Let's Encrypt to your own certificate, or the reverse
./liberty ssl off               # back to plain HTTP on port 80
```

Only the HTTPS part of the recorded compose files changes: the licensed apps and every secret stay as they are, and the stack is restarted. HTTPS needs the full layout; the light layout has no Traefik.

---

## The Traefik dashboard \{#dashboard\}

`/traefik` shows the routes and services Traefik knows about. It is protected by the user `admin` and a random password printed once by the installation.

```bash
./liberty dashboard-password      # new random password, printed once
```

`.env` keeps only the hash of the password. `./liberty doctor` reports an install that still uses the old common default password.

---

## Using your own reverse proxy \{#own-proxy\}

When a company proxy or load balancer already terminates HTTPS, keep Liberty Next on plain HTTP (`./liberty ssl off`, or the light layout) and point the proxy at it. The proxy must:

- forward WebSocket upgrades on `/socket.io` (live updates: the notification bell, record locks, assistant replies);
- keep a user on the same backend if there are several (Traefik does it with the `liberty_sticky` cookie).

---

## Liberty Next — Bundled visual tools
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/installation/portainer/

How to use the Portainer and pgAdmin instances that ship with the Liberty Full Docker layout — first-run setup, common operator tasks, Docker socket security trade-offs, Swarm specifics.

The [Full Docker layout](./docker.md#full) and [Swarm layout](./docker.md#swarm) ship with two visual ops tools pre-wired behind Traefik:

| Tool | Path | What it's for |
|---|---|---|
| [Portainer CE](https://www.portainer.io) | `/portainer` | Container-level UI — see every service, tail logs, restart, exec a shell, browse volumes. |
| [pgAdmin](https://www.pgadmin.org) | `/pgadmin` | Postgres GUI — browse schemas, run SQL, inspect query plans, manage roles. |

No separate install, no extra compose file. Bring up the Full or Swarm stack and both tools are live on the same host name as Liberty itself.

:::info[Not in the Light layout]
The Light layout is a single container with a SQLite DB — no Postgres, no Traefik. Portainer and pgAdmin only ship with the Full and Swarm layouts. If you started on Light and want these tools, move to [Full](./docker.md#full).
:::

---

## At a glance

---

## What you get out of the box

Open the host in a browser and Traefik routes the three paths:

| Path | Behind it | First-run state |
|---|---|---|
| `/` *(catchall)* | liberty-next | Sign in with `admin` + `LIBERTY_ADMIN_PASSWORD` from `.env`. |
| `/portainer` | Portainer CE | Empty — first browser visit becomes the admin-setup wizard. |
| `/pgadmin` | pgAdmin 4 | Sign in with `admin@liberty.fr` (`PGADMIN_EMAIL`) + `PGADMIN_PASSWORD` from `.env`. |

`./liberty install full` generates random secrets for both passwords on first run and stores them in `.env` mode `0600`. Read them once with `grep -E '^(PGADMIN_PASSWORD|LIBERTY_ADMIN_PASSWORD)=' .env`.

---

## Portainer — first run

1. Open `http://<host>/portainer` (or `https://` once [TLS is wired](./traefik.md)).
2. The page is the **initial admin-setup wizard** — Portainer treats the first visitor as the bootstrap operator. Create the admin account: username (often `admin`) + a 12+ character password.
3. The local Docker endpoint is auto-detected (the compose mounts the socket — see below). No need to add an environment.
4. Skip the licensing prompt — Community Edition is free for self-hosted use.

After the wizard, the dashboard lists every container running on the host. The Liberty stack shows up as the `liberty` Compose project (or `liberty` Swarm stack).

:::warning[The first visit IS the admin setup]
If the URL sits exposed before someone you trust visits it, the first stranger to reach it claims the admin account. Open the URL yourself right after `./liberty install full` finishes, or block public access at the firewall until you've completed the wizard.
:::

---

## The Docker socket mount — what makes Portainer work

Portainer needs to talk to the Docker daemon to inspect and manage containers. The bundled service does this with a bind-mount of the host socket:

```yaml title="docker-compose.full.yml (portainer service)"
portainer:
  image: portainer/portainer-ce:latest
  restart: unless-stopped
  command: -H unix:///var/run/docker.sock
  volumes:
    - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock   # privileged surface
    - portainer-data:/data
  labels:
    - "traefik.enable=true"
    - "traefik.http.routers.portainer.rule=PathPrefix(`/portainer`)"
    - "traefik.http.routers.portainer.priority=100"
    - "traefik.http.services.portainer.loadbalancer.server.port=9000"
    - "traefik.http.middlewares.portainer-strip.stripprefix.prefixes=/portainer"
    - "traefik.http.routers.portainer.middlewares=portainer-strip"
```

The Docker socket is a **privileged surface**: anything that can read it has root-equivalent control over every container on the host, including the ability to read environment variables (master key, JWT secret, Postgres password) from a running Liberty container.

| Implication | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| A Portainer admin = root over every container on the host. | Pick a strong admin password during the wizard; rotate it via *My account → Change password*. |
| Anyone who can reach `/portainer` over the network can attempt to claim it. | Restrict the path at the edge (firewall, [Traefik basic-auth middleware](./traefik.md), IP allow-list) until TLS + a real admin exists. |
| You may not want this surface in the stack at all. | Delete the `portainer:` service block plus the `portainer-data:` volume from `docker-compose.full.yml` and `docker compose up -d`. The rest of the stack is unaffected. |

The `portainer-data` named volume holds Portainer's own DB — admin account, settings, endpoint definitions. `backup.sh` snapshots it.

---

## What you can do from the bundled Portainer

Click **Containers** in the left nav. The Full layout shows five services:

| Service | At-a-glance |
|---|---|
| `liberty-next` | Status, ports, restart count, image tag. |
| `pg` | Postgres health, volume size, port. |
| `pgadmin` | Status — and yes, you can manage pgAdmin from Portainer (or vice versa). |
| `portainer` | Itself — meta-management. |
| `traefik` | Edge router status + the live dashboard link. |

Common operations:

| Task | Where in Portainer | CLI equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| Tail logs from any service | Containers → *service* → *Logs* (auto-refresh, filter by level) | `docker compose logs -f <service>` |
| Restart a service | Containers → *service* → *Restart* | `docker compose restart <service>` |
| Recreate a service (pull new image first) | Containers → *service* → *Recreate* → tick *Pull latest image* | `docker compose pull <service> && docker compose up -d <service>` |
| Open a shell inside a container | Containers → *service* → *Console* → *Connect* | `docker compose exec <service> bash` |
| Inspect environment variables (read-only) | Containers → *service* → *Inspect* tab → `Config.Env` | `docker inspect <container>` |
| Check resource usage (CPU / RAM) | Containers → *service* → *Stats* | `docker stats` |
| Browse / inspect a volume | Volumes → *volume* → *Browse* | `docker run --rm -it -v <vol>:/data alpine sh` |

Environment variables shown in Portainer are **read-only** — changing them needs an edit to `.env` followed by a recreate. The values displayed include secrets (master key, JWT secret); treat the Portainer admin login accordingly.

---

## pgAdmin — first run

Same single URL story: open `http://<host>/pgadmin` and sign in with:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Email | `admin@liberty.fr` (the default user provisioned by the compose) |
| Password | `PGADMIN_PASSWORD` from `.env` |

The compose pre-wires two things that make the path-prefixed setup work:

```yaml title="docker-compose.full.yml (pgadmin service excerpt)"
pgadmin:
  image: dpage/pgadmin4:9.18
  environment:
    PGADMIN_DEFAULT_EMAIL: "${PGADMIN_EMAIL:-admin@liberty.fr}"
    PGADMIN_DEFAULT_PASSWORD: "${PGADMIN_PASSWORD:?PGADMIN_PASSWORD is required}"
    SCRIPT_NAME: /pgadmin            # tells pgAdmin its links live under /pgadmin
  volumes:
    - pgadmin-data:/var/lib/pgadmin
  labels:
    - "traefik.enable=true"
    - "traefik.http.routers.pgadmin.rule=PathPrefix(`/pgadmin`)"
    - "traefik.http.routers.pgadmin.priority=100"
    - "traefik.http.services.pgadmin.loadbalancer.server.port=80"
```

`SCRIPT_NAME=/pgadmin` is what stops pgAdmin from generating absolute links to `/login`, `/static/...` (which would 404 because Traefik routes `/pgadmin/*` here, not `/`). Don't change it without also updating the Traefik router rule.

The `pgadmin-data` volume holds the saved server registrations, query history and preferences. `backup.sh` snapshots it.

### Register the bundled Postgres

First login lands you on an empty dashboard. Right-click **Servers → Register → Server…**:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Name (General tab) | `liberty` (anything you like) |
| Host (Connection tab) | `pg` (the compose service name — the two containers share the default network) |
| Port | `5432` |
| Username | `postgres` (or whatever `POSTGRES_USER` resolves to in `.env`) |
| Password | `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` from `.env` (tick *Save password*) |

The Liberty schema lives in the `liberty` database by default. From there it's the usual pgAdmin tree: schemas → tables → query tool.

---

## Common operator tasks via the bundled tools

| I need to… | Tool | Path |
|---|---|---|
| Tail liberty-next logs while reproducing a bug | Portainer | Containers → `liberty-next` → *Logs* → *Auto-refresh* |
| Restart Liberty after editing `.env` | Portainer | Containers → `liberty-next` → *Recreate* (so the new env is read) |
| Recreate Liberty pulling the latest image | Portainer | Containers → `liberty-next` → *Recreate* → tick *Pull latest image* |
| See how big the Postgres volume has grown | Portainer | Volumes → `pg-data` → size column |
| Run an ad-hoc `SELECT` on the Liberty DB | pgAdmin | Servers → liberty → Databases → liberty → *Query Tool* |
| Check that a migration created its table | pgAdmin | Servers → liberty → Databases → liberty → Schemas → public → Tables |
| Watch live Postgres sessions | pgAdmin | Servers → liberty → *Dashboard* → Server activity |

For everything else (admin password resets, license inspection, `liberty-admin` commands) the table in [Operations → Common tasks](./operations.md#tasks) still applies — those are CLI workflows.

---

## Swarm specifics

In the [Swarm layout](./docker.md#swarm), both Portainer and pgAdmin are deployed the same way, with two extra constraints:

| Constraint | Why |
|---|---|
| Portainer pinned to `node.role == manager` | It needs `/var/run/docker.sock`, which only managers expose. The compose sets this for you. |
| pgAdmin pinned to a manager (or wherever `pg` runs) | The `pgadmin-data` volume must reattach in place — same logic as `pg`. |

```yaml title="docker-compose.swarm.yml (portainer deploy block)"
portainer:
  image: portainer/portainer-ce:latest
  command: -H unix:///var/run/docker.sock
  volumes:
    - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock
    - portainer-data:/data
  deploy:
    replicas: 1
    placement:
      constraints:
        - node.role == manager
```

Don't try to scale Portainer beyond `replicas: 1` — it stores its admin DB on `portainer-data` and has no built-in clustering. Same for pgAdmin.

---

## Common pitfalls

| Pitfall | What actually happens | Avoid by |
|---|---|---|
| **Recreating `liberty-next` to reload a TOML edit.** | Portainer's *Recreate* kills and restarts the container — and TOML changes pushed via the Settings UI are already live. Useless restart, ~10 s of downtime. | TOMLs reload on save. The framework-wide button is `POST /admin/reload` (or *Settings → Reload*). Only recreate to apply a new image tag or a `.env` change. |
| **Restarting `pg` without first stopping `liberty-next`.** | Liberty's pool sees half its connections drop mid-query; the next requests fail until the pool recovers. | Stop `liberty-next` first (Portainer → *Stop*), restart `pg`, start `liberty-next`. Or restart the whole stack in order. |
| **Editing env vars in Portainer.** | Portainer's env tab is read-only — there's no *Save* button. Operators sometimes copy them out, edit, paste back, and nothing happens. | Edit `.env` on the host, then *Recreate* the container so the new values are read at startup. |
| **Exposing `/portainer` to the public internet before completing the wizard.** | The first stranger to load the page claims the admin account. | Run the wizard immediately after `./liberty install full`. Or firewall the path until you have. |
| **Treating the Docker socket as harmless.** | It isn't — Portainer + socket = root on every container, including Liberty's env (master key, JWT secret, DB password). | Strong Portainer admin password; consider deleting the service entirely if no one needs it. |

---

## When to remove the bundled tools

The bundled services are convenient, not mandatory. Remove them if:

- **Compliance forbids the Docker socket inside the application stack.** Delete the `portainer:` block + `portainer-data:` volume; manage Docker from a separate, locked-down host.
- **You have a central pgAdmin / DBeaver / DataGrip already.** Delete the `pgadmin:` block + `pgadmin-data:` volume; connect your central tool through an SSH tunnel to `127.0.0.1:5432` on the host (PostgreSQL is published on the loopback only).
- **You're tight on RAM (≤ 2 GB).** Each tool adds ~50–150 MB resident — small but not zero.

After removing either service:

```bash
docker compose up -d                                   # COMPOSE_FILE picks the right files; reconciles the stack
docker volume rm <removed-volume>                       # only if you're sure
```

The rest of the Liberty stack (liberty-next, pg, traefik) is unaffected.

## Liberty Next — Operations
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/installation/operations/

Run a Liberty Next install day to day: ./liberty status and doctor, start, stop and logs, backups and restores, common administrator tasks, the liberty-ops twin for Python installs, and the usual problems with their fix.

Everything an administrator does on a running install goes through one command: `./liberty` (run from `release/`) on Docker, `liberty-ops` on a Python install. Both have the same verbs.

---

## At a glance

---

## Status \{#status\}

```text title="./liberty status"
Liberty Next — /opt/liberty-next/release
  layout        full
  tls           letsencrypt (liberty.example.com)
  apps overlay  yes (/opt/liberty-next/release/apps)
  image tag     7.0.58
  chain         docker-compose.full.yml:docker-compose.tls-letsencrypt.yml:docker-compose.apps.yml
  container     running/healthy
  framework     7.0.58
  apps bundle   7.0.58
  /ready        {"status":"ok","version":"7.0.58","pool":"default"}
  migrations    up to date
  last upgrade  stack 7.0.57 → 7.0.58 (2026-10-27T08:12:40)
```

| Line | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `layout`, `tls`, `apps overlay`, `chain` | What was installed and the compose files recorded in `.env`. |
| `image tag` | `latest` or the pinned release. |
| `container` | Docker state and health — `unhealthy` when the framework database does not answer. |
| `framework`, `apps bundle` | The versions actually running. |
| `/ready` | The readiness check of the server. |
| `migrations` | Schema migrations of the licensed apps still to apply. |
| `last upgrade` | The last entry of **Settings → History → Upgrades**. |

---

## Doctor \{#doctor\}

`./liberty doctor` checks the install and prints, for each problem, the command that fixes it. It ends with exit code `1` when something is wrong — a support request starts with its output.

It checks:

- `.env`, the recorded compose files and that each one exists;
- that the licensed apps folder is in the compose files when one is configured — the usual cause of an install that "looks empty";
- the length of the master key and of the JWT secret;
- the Traefik dashboard password and the PostgreSQL port exposure (full layout);
- the certificate files or the Let's Encrypt domain when HTTPS is on;
- the volumes, the container and `/ready`;
- the pending schema migrations;
- that the master key decrypts every pool password;
- the free disk space.

---

## Start, stop, logs \{#lifecycle\}

| Command | Effect |
|---|---|
| `./liberty start` | Starts the stack with the recorded compose files and waits until it is healthy. |
| `./liberty stop` | Stops the containers. Volumes and `.env` are kept. |
| `./liberty restart` | Restarts `liberty-next` only. |
| `./liberty logs` / `logs -f` | The last 200 lines of the server log / follow it. |

Every log line written while a request is handled carries that request's id, which is also returned in the `X-Request-ID` response header: quote it to find the matching lines.toml` writes one JSON object per line.

---

## Backup and restore \{#backup\}

```bash
./liberty backup                  # → release/backups/<YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS>/
./liberty backup --keep 30        # and delete backups older than 30 days
./liberty restore backups/2026-10-27_030000
```

A backup folder holds one archive per volume (`liberty-config`, `pg-data` or `liberty-data`, `pgadmin-data`, `portainer-data`), the licensed apps folder (`liberty-apps.tar.gz`), a copy of `.env` (`.env.snapshot`, mode `0600`, with the secrets) and the compose files. A backup can run while the stack is up.

`./liberty restore` stops the stack, puts every archive of the folder back in its volume and in the apps folder, and starts again. Everything written since the backup is lost.

A weekly backup kept 60 days, from cron:

```cron
0 3 * * 0  cd /opt/liberty-next/release && ./backup.sh /mnt/backup/liberty --keep 60
```

Copy the backups off the server. `.env.snapshot` contains the master key: without it the restored configuration cannot decrypt its passwords.

---

## Common tasks \{#tasks\}

| Task | Command (Docker) |
|---|---|
| New random password for `admin` | `docker exec -u liberty liberty-next liberty-admin set-password admin` |
| Another superuser | `docker exec -u liberty liberty-next liberty-admin create-user alice --superuser` |
| Check the licence | `docker exec -u liberty liberty-next liberty-license status` |
| Apply the apps' schema migrations | `./liberty migrate` (`--dry-run` lists them) |
| Reload the configuration after editing a file | **Settings → Reload config** |
| New Traefik dashboard password | `./liberty dashboard-password` |
| A shell in the container | `docker exec -it -u liberty liberty-next bash` |

`-u liberty` matters: the server runs as `liberty`, and a command run as root would leave files the server can no longer write. `./liberty` passes it on its own. Without `--password`, `set-password` and `create-user` generate a password and print it.

---

## Python installs: liberty-ops \{#liberty-ops\}

Run as the service user with its environment loaded (`sudo -u liberty bash -c 'set -a; . /etc/liberty/secrets.env; set +a; liberty-ops status'`).

| Command | Effect |
|---|---|
| `liberty-ops status` | Versions, configuration folder, apps folder, service state, `/ready`, pending migrations, last upgrade. |
| `liberty-ops doctor` | Python version, secrets, configuration files, apps and plugins, master key, service, `/ready`, migrations, disk — each problem with its fix. |
| `liberty-ops start` · `stop` · `restart` · `logs [-f]` | The systemd unit (`liberty-next`, or `LIBERTY_SERVICE`). |
| `liberty-ops backup [--dest DIR] [--keep DAYS]` | Configuration folder (with its history), apps folder, the SQLite file, and a `pg_dump` when the default pool is PostgreSQL and `pg_dump` is installed. Default destination: `backups/` next to the configuration folder. |
| `liberty-ops restore <dir> [--yes]` | Puts a backup back, stopping and starting the service around it. A PostgreSQL dump is not restored automatically: the command to run is printed. |
| `liberty-ops migrate [--dry-run]` | The apps' schema migrations. |
| `liberty-ops upgrade` · `rollback` | See [Upgrade and rollback](./upgrading.md#python). |

---

## Troubleshooting \{#troubleshooting\}

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| The install looks empty after an upgrade or a restart | The container was recreated without the licensed apps folder (a `docker compose -f …` by hand). | `./liberty doctor`, then `./liberty apps <wheel>` — and keep to `./liberty` commands. |
| `docker ps` shows `liberty-next` **unhealthy** | The framework database does not answer `/ready`. | `./liberty logs`; on the full layout check the `liberty-pg` container. |
| Sign-in answers *Too many failed logins — try again in N s* | Ten failed sign-ins in five minutes for that user (see [Sign-in](../framework/build/secure/sign-in.md)). | Wait for the time given, or reset the password. |
| Pools fail with a decryption error | `LIBERTY_MASTER_KEY` is not the key the passwords were encrypted with. | Put back the original key (see `.env.snapshot` in a backup). |
| The server says schema migrations are pending | A new apps release brings database changes. | `./liberty migrate`. |
| A file changed on disk is not taken into account | Files are read at start-up or on reload. | **Settings → Reload config**. |
| Port 80 or 8000 already used | Another service holds it. | Set `TRAEFIK_HTTP_PORT` (full) or `LIBERTY_PORT` (light) in `.env`, then `./liberty start`. |
| The install refuses to start: *stale Docker volumes* | Volumes of a previous install exist but its `.env` is gone. | Restore the old `.env`, or `./liberty install --reset` then install again. |

---

## Liberty Next — Upgrade and rollback
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/installation/upgrading/

Upgrade Liberty Next with one command: ./liberty upgrade (Docker) or liberty-ops upgrade (Python) checks the install, takes a backup, installs the new release and the apps, applies the schema migrations and records a report; rollback undoes it. Swarm upgrades and versioning.

An upgrade is one command. It never starts without a fresh backup, keeps what is needed to come back, and leaves a report you can read in the application.

---

## At a glance

---

## Docker \{#docker\}

```bash
cd liberty-next/release
git pull                                  # the scripts of the new release
./liberty upgrade                         # to the latest release
./liberty upgrade --tag 7.0.58            # or to a given release (kept in .env)
```

What the command does, in order:

| Step | Detail |
|---|---|
| 1. Check | Runs `doctor`. Problems are reported but do not stop the upgrade — an upgrade is often what fixes them. |
| 2. Keep the image | The image now running is tagged locally `rollback-<date>` so that it can be started again. |
| 3. Backup | `backup` of every volume and of the apps folder, kept `--keep` days (30 by default). **If the backup fails, the upgrade stops and nothing is changed.** |
| 4. Pull and recreate | The new image is pulled and the containers recreated with the recorded compose files — HTTPS and the licensed apps stay in place. |
| 5. Apps and migrations | With `--apps <wheel>`, the new apps bundle is installed (with its [merge plan](./deploy-prebuilt-apps.md#merge)); then the pending schema migrations are applied. |
| 6. Report | The report is recorded and `status` is printed. |

Downtime is the time the container takes to restart, usually well under a minute.

### Upgrading the licensed apps \{#apps\}

```bash
./liberty upgrade --apps ./liberty_apps-7.0.58-py3-none-any.whl
```

Framework and apps are upgraded in one run. To refresh the apps alone, without a new framework image: `./liberty apps <wheel>`.

---

## Python install \{#python\}

```bash
liberty-ops upgrade                                       # framework to the latest release
liberty-ops upgrade --version 7.0.58                      # a given release
liberty-ops upgrade --apps ./liberty_apps-7.0.58-py3-none-any.whl
```

Same sequence: `doctor` → backup (the only step that can stop the upgrade) → `pipx upgrade` (or the pinned version) → the apps wheel → `liberty-admin migrate` → service restart and wait for `/ready` → report → `status`. `--no-restart` leaves the restart to you; `--backup-dest` chooses where the backup goes.

Run it as the service user with its environment loaded, as for every `liberty-ops` command.

---

## The upgrade report \{#report\}

Each `upgrade` and each `rollback` records a report: versions before and after, image tag, compose files, backup folder, `doctor` findings, the result of every step and the migrations applied. It is stored with the configuration (`.versions/upgrades/`), and on Docker a copy is also written in the backup folder.

Open it in **Settings → History → Upgrades**. Each entry shows its component:

| Entry | Recorded by |
|---|---|
| **Stack** | `./liberty upgrade`, `./liberty rollback`, `liberty-ops upgrade` — the report described above. |
| **Framework**, **Apps** | A change of version noticed when the server starts — shown with the release notes of the new version. |
| **`<app>` schema** | `liberty-admin migrate` — the migrations applied to an application database. |
| `framework-schema` | Columns the server added to its own tables when a new release needed them. |

---

## Schema migrations \{#migrations\}

The framework creates and completes its own tables when it starts. The licensed apps' databases change through **migrations** shipped in the apps wheel:

- `./liberty upgrade` and `liberty-ops upgrade` apply them;
- `./liberty status`, `./liberty doctor` and the server log at start-up say when some are pending;
- `./liberty migrate --dry-run` lists them, `./liberty migrate` applies them;
- with `LIBERTY_AUTO_MIGRATE=1` in `.env`, the server applies them itself at start-up.

Every run is recorded in **Settings → History → Upgrades**. For a database whose recorded version is ahead of its real tables, `liberty-admin migrate --app nomasx1 --stamp <revision>` sets the version without running anything, then applies what remains — see [CLI](../references/cli.md#migrate).

---

## Rollback \{#rollback\}

```bash
./liberty rollback            # asks for confirmation
./liberty rollback --yes
```

The command starts again the image kept before the last upgrade and restores the backup taken just before it. **Everything written since that backup is lost** — hence the confirmation. The report of the upgrade is kept, and the rollback gets its own.

On a Python install, `liberty-ops rollback` reinstalls the previous framework version and restores the backup taken before the upgrade. pipx keeps no copy of the previous apps wheel: pass it with `--apps <previous wheel>` to downgrade the apps too.

To go back further than the last upgrade: `./liberty restore <backup folder>` and `./liberty upgrade --tag <release>`.

---

## Docker Swarm \{#swarm\}

`./liberty` does not drive a swarm. Take a backup with `./backup.sh`, then:

```bash
docker service update --image ghcr.io/fblettner/liberty-next:7.0.58 liberty_liberty-next
docker exec -u liberty $(docker ps -qf name=liberty_liberty-next) liberty-admin migrate
docker service rollback liberty_liberty-next      # if something is wrong
```

Or set `LIBERTY_IMAGE_TAG` in `.env` and run `./deploy-swarm.sh` again.

---

## Versions \{#versions\}

| Change | What to expect |
|---|---|
| Patch (`7.0.57` → `7.0.58`) | Fixes and features; the configuration stays compatible; database changes only add tables or columns. |
| A larger step | The release notes say what to check before and after. |

Read the release notes before upgrading: **Settings → Release notes** shows those of the running version.

---

## Tips \{#tips\}

- Pin the release in production (`--tag`) and upgrade on purpose, a test server first.
- Run `./liberty doctor` before the upgrade: a problem reported there is easier to fix before than after.
- After the upgrade, sign in, open a screen of each application and run a Nomaflow job by hand.
- Keep the backup of the upgrade until the next one has run.

---

## Liberty Next — Production checklist
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/installation/production/

What to check before a Liberty Next server goes into production: pinned release, HTTPS, passwords, secrets kept off the server, exposed ports, sign-in protection, backups, logs, monitoring — and what the shipped Docker layouts already harden for you.

The shipped layouts are already hardened; this page lists what they do for you and what is left to decide before users arrive. `./liberty doctor` (or `liberty-ops doctor`) checks most of it — run it last.

---

## Already done by the Docker layouts \{#built-in\}

| Protection | Detail |
|---|---|
| The server does not run as root | The container fixes the ownership of its volumes, then runs as `liberty` (uid 1000). `LIBERTY_RUN_AS_ROOT=1` turns this off. |
| PostgreSQL is not on the network | Published on `127.0.0.1` only. `POSTGRES_BIND=0.0.0.0` in `.env` opens it — then protect it with a firewall. |
| Random secrets per install | Master key, JWT secret, PostgreSQL, pgAdmin and Traefik dashboard passwords are generated by the installation. |
| HTTPS done properly | With `./liberty ssl …`, HTTP is redirected to HTTPS and security headers are sent. |
| Health that means something | The healthcheck asks the database (`/ready`), not just the process. |
| Sign-in throttle | After 10 failed sign-ins for a user within 5 minutes (50 from one address), sign-in answers *429* for a while. See [Sign-in](../framework/build/secure/sign-in.md#throttle). |
| No SQL in error messages | Regular users get the database error line and an error id; the statement itself goes to the log only when the pool's `debug_sql` is on. |
| Known images | Every image is pinned to a version, and each release is scanned for known vulnerabilities before publication. |

---

## Before going live \{#checklist\}

- [ ] **Pin the release**: `./liberty upgrade --tag <version>` — never `latest` in production. See [Upgrade and rollback](./upgrading.md).
- [ ] **HTTPS on**: `./liberty ssl letsencrypt …` or `provided …`, or your own proxy in front. See [HTTPS and Traefik](./traefik.md).
- [ ] **Passwords changed and stored**: the `admin` password (`liberty-admin set-password admin`), the pgAdmin and Traefik dashboard passwords printed by the installation.
- [ ] **Secrets kept off the server**: a copy of `release/.env` (or `secrets.env`) in your vault. Without the master key, a restored configuration cannot decrypt its passwords. For Docker or Kubernetes secrets, give `LIBERTY_MASTER_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/…` instead of the value.
- [ ] **Licence** pasted in **Settings → App → License**, and its expiry date noted.
- [ ] **Sign-in**: OpenID Connect set up if the company has an identity provider ([Sign-in](../framework/build/secure/sign-in.md)); a second superuser so that one lost password does not lock the install.
- [ ] **Roles** reviewed: who sees which menus, and which rows ([Roles and permissions](../framework/build/secure/roles-and-permissions.md)).
- [ ] **Backups scheduled and copied off the server** ([Operations](./operations.md#backup)), and **one restore tested**.
- [ ] **Tools**: Portainer and pgAdmin are reachable on the same address as the application. Remove them from the stack, or restrict them in Traefik, if nobody needs them.
- [ ] **Notifications**: the SMTP account in **Settings → App → Notifications (email)** and a rule for failed jobs ([Notifications](../nomaflow/notifications.md)).
- [ ] **Monitoring**: an external probe on `/ready` ([Health endpoints](../monitoring/health-endpoints.md)).
- [ ] **`./liberty doctor` answers *no problems found***.

---

## Logs \{#logs\}

- Every response carries an `X-Request-ID` header, and every log line written for that request carries the same id: give it when reporting a problem.
- The container log is rotated by Docker for PostgreSQL (3 × 100 MB). For the other containers, set a rotation in the Docker daemon (`/etc/docker/daemon.json`).

---

## Keep one replica \{#replicas\}

Live updates (the notification bell, record locks, the assistant's answers) are held in the server process, and the sign-in throttle counts per process. Run **one** `liberty-next` instance: several replicas would show users different states.

---

## Liberty Next — Step 1 — Set up the CRM project
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/tutorial-crm/setup/

Start the Build-a-CRM tutorial: the tables for customers, deals and activities, sample data, and the crm connector that will become the app. End state: the framework running, a superuser signed in, the tables ready.

This tutorial builds a small **customer relationship management** app on Liberty Next, in six steps: screens, lists of values, a dashboard, roles, the AI assistant and a scheduled job. Everything is done from Settings.

This first step prepares the database and creates the `crm` connector.

---

## At a glance

---

## What we're building

| Step | We add | What it teaches |
|---|---|---|
| **1 — Setup** *(this page)* | Tables, sample data, the `crm` connector. | Pools and connectors. |
| **[2 — Customers](./02-customers.md)** | The Customers screen and the app's menu. | Queries generated from a table, screens, menus. |
| **[3 — Deals](./03-deals.md)** | Deals linked to customers, with their activities in a tab. | Dictionary, lists of values, nested tabs. |
| **[4 — Dashboard](./04-dashboard.md)** | A pipeline dashboard. | KPIs, charts, the period. |
| **[5 — Roles](./05-auth.md)** | Roles, users, a data scope, company sign-in. | Who sees what. |
| **[6 — AI and jobs](./06-ai-and-jobs.md)** | The AI assistant and a daily job. | Assistant, Nomaflow, notifications. |

---

## Prerequisites

| Need | Why |
|---|---|
| **Liberty Next installed** | See [Installation](../../installation/overview.md). |
| **A superuser account** | Settings is reserved to superusers. |
| **A SQL client** | To create the tables — `psql`, DBeaver, or any client connected to the database of the `default` pool. |

The `default` pool points at the bundled PostgreSQL database on a Docker install, or at a local SQLite file on a Python install without PostgreSQL. The SQL below is written for PostgreSQL; on SQLite, replace `SERIAL` with `INTEGER`.

---

## Create the tables

```sql
CREATE TABLE customers (
  id            SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  name          VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  industry      VARCHAR(64),
  country       VARCHAR(2),
  status        VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE',
  primary_email VARCHAR(255),
  created_by    VARCHAR(64),
  created_at    TIMESTAMP,
  updated_by    VARCHAR(64),
  updated_at    TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE TABLE deal_stages (
  code  VARCHAR(16) PRIMARY KEY,
  label VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
  ord   INTEGER NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE deals (
  id          SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
  name        VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  stage       VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'QUALIFIED' REFERENCES deal_stages(code),
  amount      DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  close_date  DATE,
  owner       VARCHAR(64),
  updated_at  TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE TABLE activities (
  id          SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  deal_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES deals(id),
  kind        VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL,
  notes       VARCHAR(2000),
  happened_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  recorded_by VARCHAR(64)
);

INSERT INTO deal_stages (code, label, ord) VALUES
  ('QUALIFIED', 'Qualified', 10), ('PROPOSAL', 'Proposal', 20),
  ('NEGOTIATION', 'Negotiation', 30), ('WON', 'Won', 40), ('LOST', 'Lost', 50);

INSERT INTO customers (name, industry, country, primary_email) VALUES
  ('ACME Industries', 'Manufacturing', 'FR', 'contact@acme.example'),
  ('Beta SARL',       'Logistics',     'FR', 'sales@beta.example'),
  ('Gamma SA',        'Services',      'BE', 'hello@gamma.example');

INSERT INTO deals (customer_id, name, stage, amount, close_date) VALUES
  (1, 'Annual contract renewal', 'PROPOSAL',     45000, '2026-11-15'),
  (1, 'Training package',        'QUALIFIED',     8500, '2026-12-10'),
  (2, 'Logistics platform',      'NEGOTIATION', 120000, '2026-11-30'),
  (3, 'Support contract',        'WON',          18000, '2026-10-05');
```

---

## Create the `crm` connector

A **connector** groups the queries of one database under a name. Once it has a menu, it becomes the `crm` **app**.

1. Open **Settings → Connectors**, click **＋ Connector**.
2. Name `crm`, type **SQL**, pool `default`. Save.

The connector appears under *Data sources* in the left list: it has no menu yet. It moves to *Apps* in [Step 2](./02-customers.md).

To work on another database than the framework's, first add a pool in **Settings → Pools** with its URL, then pick it here — see [Connectors](../connectors.md#pools).

---

## Check

| Check | How |
|---|---|
| Tables created | `SELECT count(*) FROM customers;` returns 3. |
| Connector created | **Settings → Connectors** lists `crm` under *Data sources*. |

→ **[Step 2 — Customers](./02-customers.md)**: the queries, the first screen and the menu.
