## Liberty Next — Dashboards
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/dashboards/

Liberty Next dashboards: KPIs, charts and tables over connector queries on a 12-column grid, a period with presets and comparison with the previous period, dictionary filters, a cache with Refresh — built in Settings → Dashboards and opened from the menu.

A dashboard puts several **widgets** — figures, charts, tables — side by side, each fed by a query of a connector. It opens from the menu like a screen, and it is built in **Settings → Dashboards**.

---

## At a glance

---

## Widgets \{#widgets\}

Widgets sit on a 12-column grid, in the order they are declared. Each one takes a width of 1 to 12 columns and a height of 1 to 8 rows, and may carry a title.

| Widget | Shows | Settings |
|---|---|---|
| **KPI** | One figure computed over every row of a query. | Connector, query, column, aggregation (`count`, `sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, or `none` for the first row's value), format, and **compare with the previous period**. |
| **Chart** | A bar, line, area or pie chart. | A chart saved in **Settings → Charts**, or a connector, a query and a chart definition written in the widget — see [Charts](./charts.md). |
| **Table** | The rows of a query. | Connector, query, the columns to show (all when empty), a row limit. |

A widget whose query the user may not run is hidden; the rest of the dashboard still shows.

---

## The period \{#period\}

A dashboard can carry a **period**: a date range control in its bar that applies to every widget.

- **Presets**: Today, Yesterday, Last 7 days, Last 30 days, This month, Last month, This quarter, This year, Last year, Last 12 months, All dates. The *Yesterday* preset covers yesterday and today.
- **A free range**: pick a start date, then an end date, in the two-month calendar, then **Apply**.
- **Date basis**: when the dashboard offers several dates (*Document date*, *Paid on*), a **Date** choice at the bottom of the panel picks the one the range applies to.

The dashboard opens on its own default preset, otherwise on the application's default (**Settings → App → Default period (dashboards)**, *This month* by default). A choice lasts as long as the dashboard tab stays open.

### What the queries receive

| Bind | Value |
|---|---|
| `:PERIOD_FROM`, `:PERIOD_TO` | The chosen range, as dates. *All dates* binds `0001-01-01` to `9999-12-31`. |
| `:PREV_FROM`, `:PREV_TO` | The period before (see below). |
| `:PERIOD_BASIS` | The chosen date basis, when the dashboard offers several. |

A query that does not mention them is not affected. When the period names its date column — directly or through a dictionary item found in the widget's screen — the widget is also filtered on the server on that column, **without any change to its SQL**.

### The previous period

| Range | Compared with |
|---|---|
| Starting on 1 January (*This year*, *Last year*) | The same dates one year earlier. |
| Starting on the 1st of a month | The same number of months just before — *Last month* with the month before, a whole quarter with the quarter before; *This month* on the 27th with the 1st–27th of the previous month. |
| Anything else | The same number of days just before. |

### Comparing a KPI

With **Compare with the previous period** ticked, a KPI runs its query a second time on the previous period and shows, under the figure, the change — in percent, in points for a percent KPI — in green or red, and the previous value. Nothing is compared on *All dates*.

---

## Filters \{#filters\}

A dashboard can also carry **filters**, shown as dropdowns in its bar. Each filter has a label, a dictionary item and a query that provides its choices (value column and label column), and an optional default value. Choosing a value reloads every widget whose screen has a column carrying that dictionary item; the other widgets are left as they are.

---

## Refresh and cache \{#cache\}

When a dashboard is opened again, each widget reuses its last result for **Settings → App → Dashboard cache (seconds, 0 = none)** — 60 seconds by default. The **↻** button in the bar reloads everything, and *Updated at 14:05* says when the data was fetched. The cache is kept in the browser, per user, until the page is reloaded.

---

## Building a dashboard \{#builder\}

In **Settings → Dashboards**, pick the application, then add or open a dashboard. The editor has:

| Part | Content |
|---|---|
| General | Title, description. |
| Period | **Add a period**: *Opens on* (a preset, or *App default*), *Date column* or *dictionary item*, and optional **Date bases** (key, label, date column or dictionary item). |
| Filters | The dropdowns of the bar. |
| Widgets | **Add widget**: Chart, KPI or Table. Each widget has buttons to make it narrower or wider (W−, W+), lower or taller (H−, H+), and to move it earlier or later in the grid. |

The editor's labels are in English. To make the dashboard reachable, add a **dashboard** entry to a menu ([Menus](./build/menus/item-types.md)); its permission is `dashboard:<app>.<id>`.

### In TOML

```toml title="dashboards.toml"
[dashboards.sales.overview]
label = "Sales overview"
period = { column = "DOC_DATE", default = "thisMonth" }

  [[dashboards.sales.overview.widgets]]
  type = "kpi"
  label = "Revenue"
  connector = "sales"
  query = "revenue_by_company_get"
  column = "REVENUE"
  aggregation = "sum"
  compare_previous = true
  col_span = 4

  [[dashboards.sales.overview.widgets]]
  type = "chart"
  chart = "revenue_by_month"
  col_span = 8
  row_span = 2
```

---

## Tips \{#tips\}

- Give the dashboard a period rather than date filters in each query: one control, and the comparison comes for free.
- A KPI with `none` shows the first row's value: let the query compute the figure when the aggregation is complex.
- Keep the cache on for dashboards opened often; **↻** always gives fresh figures.

---

## Liberty Next — Charts
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/charts/

A saved chart draws the result of a connector query as bars, lines, areas or a pie: an X column, one or more series with their colour and axis, and an aggregation. Built in Settings → Charts or saved from a screen's Chart view, then reused in dashboards.

A **chart** draws the result of a connector's query: an X column, one or more series, and an aggregation for the rows that share the same X value. It is saved under a name and reused in [dashboards](./dashboards.md); the same chart settings are available on the fly in a screen's **Chart** view.

Four types are available: **bar**, **line**, **area** and **pie**.

---

## At a glance

---

## Settings → Charts \{#list\}

Charts are grouped by connector: the **scope** chips at the top pick a connector, and **Add a connector scope** opens a new one. The list shows each chart of the scope with its label, its id and an *override* badge when it is marked as a local customisation. Each row has:

| Button | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Find usages** | The dashboards that show the chart. |
| **Find dependencies** | Lists what the chart depends on (query, connector…) and downloads the chart with the ticked items as a package. |
| **Rename** | Changes the chart's id. |
| **Clone** | Copies the chart under a new id. |
| **Delete** | Removes the chart. |

**Add chart** opens the editor for a new chart in the current scope; clicking a row opens it for editing.

---

## The editor \{#editor\}

The editor has two tabs.

### General \{#general\}

| Field | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Id** | The chart's identifier: letters, digits, underscores and hyphens. Dashboards refer to the chart by this id. |
| **Label** | The chart's title in lists and dashboards. |
| **Description** | Optional. |
| **Connector** | The connector of the scope — fixed; to move a chart to another connector, recreate it in that scope. |
| **Query** | The read query whose result the chart draws. The buttons next to it edit the query, clone it or create a new one without leaving the editor. |

### Chart \{#chart\}

The tab loads a sample of the query's rows and draws the chart as it is set:

| Field | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Chart** | The type: bar, line, area or pie. |
| **X axis** | The column along the X axis — the slice labels on a pie. |
| **Series** | One line per Y column: the column, a colour swatch, and **L** / **R** to put the series on the left or the right Y axis. **+** adds a series. A pie uses the first series only. |
| **Aggregate** | How rows sharing the same X value are combined: **Sum**, **Average**, **Count** (counts rows, ignores the Y value), **Min**, **Max**, or **None (per row)** to keep each row — for a time series whose X is already unique. |

As soon as one series is on the right axis, the chart gets a second Y axis — useful for two scales, such as an amount and a count. The legend shows when there is more than one series. Without a colour, a series takes the next colour of the palette.

An X column and at least one series are required to save.

---

## From a screen's Chart view \{#from-a-screen\}

The **Chart** button of a screen switches the grid to a chart of the rows on display, with the same settings (type, X axis, series, aggregation). Two extras appear there:

- **Load saved** — applies a saved chart built on the same connector and query;
- **Save…** — saves the current chart under an id, a label and a description, ready for dashboards. Only a superuser sees this button.

---

## In a dashboard \{#in-a-dashboard\}

A dashboard's **Chart** widget shows a saved chart by its id, or holds its own chart definition. A change to the saved chart shows on every dashboard that uses it. See [Dashboards](./dashboards.md).

---

## Upgrades \{#override\}

The *override* badge flags a chart marked as a local customisation: an upgrade package does not overwrite it. See [Packages](./build/packages.md).

---

- [Dashboards](./dashboards.md) — put charts, figures and tables side by side.
- [Connectors](./connectors.md) — the queries a chart reads.
- [Saved views](./saved-views.md) — what a user can keep from a screen.

## Liberty Next — Data Explorer
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/explorer/overview/

The Liberty Next Data Explorer: free analysis of an app's data without writing SQL — fields pane, rows, measures and filters, a period, table, pivot, charts and KPI views, detail rows and drill, calculated fields, saved analyses, dashboards and Excel / PDF export, over a model built in Settings → Explorer.

The Data Explorer lets users analyse an app's data on their own: they pick fields, group, filter, choose a period, then read the result as a table, a pivot, a chart or KPI cards — without writing a query. It works on any connected application whose data is reached through a SQL connector.

An operator first describes the data once, as a **model**, in **Settings → Explorer**. Users then open the explorer from the **compass** in the header, which appears when at least one model is available to them.

---

## At a glance

---

## The pieces \{#pieces\}

| Piece | What it is | Page |
|---|---|---|
| **Model** | One data mart of an app: a central entity (the **hub**, such as deals or invoice lines) and the entities around it (customers, activities…), each read by a query of a connector, joined by relations. An app can have several models. | [Build a model](./model.md) |
| **Analysis** | What the user puts together on the page: rows, measures, filters, a period, a view. | [Analyse data](./analysis.md) |
| **Calculated field** | A field computed from the others (`AMOUNT * 0.6`, `year(CLOSE_DATE)`), typed and checked on the server. | [Calculated fields](./calculated-fields.md) |
| **Saved analysis, dashboard** | An analysis kept under a name, private or shared; a dashboard is a grid of saved analyses. Both export to Excel and PDF. | [Saved analyses and dashboards](./saved-and-dashboards.md) |

---

## Who sees what \{#access\}

- A model is offered to the holders of a role that grants it: in **Settings → Access → Roles**, **Beyond the menus**, type **Data Explorer**, then a model, or every model of an app. Superusers see every model. See [Roles & permissions](../build/secure/roles-and-permissions.md#access).
- The role's **data scope** applies inside every query the explorer runs: a user who sees one company's rows in the screens sees the same rows in the explorer, the totals included. See [Data scope](../build/secure/roles-and-permissions.md#data-scope).
- Only a superuser edits **Settings → Explorer**, and sees the SQL of an analysis and the model's warnings (a column that disappeared, a measure that is not numeric).

---

## What it is not \{#limits\}

- **Not a SQL editor.** Users never type SQL: the explorer builds one statement from the model, the same on Oracle, PostgreSQL and SQLite. A calculated field is a small expression language, compiled by the server.
- **Not unlimited.** An aggregate reads at most 50,000 grouped rows (beyond that, a note says the figures are partial) and shows the **Top** N groups (up to 10,000). The detail view pages through the rows; an export holds up to 3,000 rows per section.
- **Not a replacement for dashboards.** [Dashboards](../dashboards.md) are designed by an operator over chosen queries; the explorer lets users build their own views over a model.

---

## What's next

- [Build a model](./model.md) — Settings → Explorer, from scratch or from a Screen Assistant preset.
- [Analyse data](./analysis.md) — the page, step by step.

---

## Liberty Next — Build a model
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/explorer/model/

Settings → Explorer in Liberty Next: an explorer model per data mart — the hub, the entities (a query with its cardinality, key, measures, hidden columns and default date), the relations on column pairs, and a model filled from a Screen Assistant preset.

A model tells the explorer what a user may analyse and how the tables relate. It is built in **Settings → Explorer** by a superuser, with no SQL: every entity reads an existing query of a connector, and the columns are discovered from that query's result.

---

## At a glance

---

## The app and the model \{#app-model\}

1. **App** — the bar at the top lists the apps that already have a model; **+ Add an app** offers the SQL connectors that have none.
2. **Model** — pick a model of the app, or **Add model** and give its id (letters, digits, `_` and `-`). An app can hold several models: tables that do not relate to one another belong in different models. **Delete model** removes it with its entities and relations.
3. The header of the model:

| Field | Use |
|---|---|
| **Label** | The name users see in the explorer's model picker. |
| **Hub** | The entity every analysis starts from: a fact table, a document header, the lines of a document. |
| **Description** | Shown under the explorer's title. |
| **Preset (Screen Assistant)** | Fills the model from a preset — see [below](#preset). |

**Save** writes the model and reloads it: the explorer sees it at once. A model without any entity is not saved.

---

## Entities \{#entities\}

**Add entity** (or a click on an entity) opens its form:

| Field | Use |
|---|---|
| **Id** | The entity's identifier, fixed once created (`deals`, `customers`). |
| **Label** | The name of the group in the fields pane. |
| **Rows per hub row** | **1..1 · one** — at most one row per hub row (the customer of a deal); **1..n · many** — several rows (the activities of a deal). The hub itself is always 1..1. |
| **Description** | Free text. |
| **Connector** | The connector of the query; the app's own by default. |
| **Query** | A SELECT query of that connector, without parameters. Its columns are discovered by running it for one row. |
| **Screen (column hints)** | A screen whose column settings give the labels, formats and lists of values. The screens that read the same query come first. |
| **Default date** | The date field the period applies to first. |

The **Columns** table lists the discovered columns, with the label and the type taken from the screen. For each one:

- **Key** — the columns that identify a row. A new entity takes the screen's key columns. The key opens a row in its screen's dialog from the detail view.
- **Measure** — a numeric column that users sum, average, count…: pick its default aggregate (`sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, `count`, `count_distinct`). Left on *— dimension —*, the column groups and filters.
- **Hidden** — left out of the fields pane. A column hidden by the screen stays hidden.

A column that the query no longer returns is flagged with **?** so it can be unticked.

### What users get from a column \{#fields\}

Each column becomes a **field** of the pane, labelled and formatted through the dictionary and the screen, and typed as text, number, date, date-time or yes/no. A column with a list of values (an enum or a lookup in the screen) shows its labels and offers its values in the filters. A column declared as a measure but not numeric stays a dimension, and the model reports it to superusers.

---

## Relations \{#relations\}

A relation joins two entities on one or more **column pairs**: `customers` → `deals` on `ID = CUSTOMER_ID`. **Add relation**, pick both entities, then the columns (the lists show each entity's columns; a name can also be typed); **+** adds a pair for a composite key.

Every entity must reach the hub, directly or through other entities. The explorer then picks the joins an analysis needs, and never multiplies rows twice: an analysis groups by at most one 1..n entity, and the others are reached without duplicating the hub's rows.

---

## A model from a preset \{#preset\}

A Screen Assistant preset already declares a set of tables and their joins. Picking it in **Preset (Screen Assistant)** fills the model:

- every table of the preset becomes an entity (all its columns, or the preset's own column list), the base table the hub;
- the joins become relations, matched on the real columns — the column of that name, the one carrying that dictionary item, or, on a connector with a table prefix (JD Edwards EnterpriseOne: `ABAN8`, `WWAN8`), the one whose name without the prefix is the item.

Entities already declared are kept and completed; a key, measures, a default date or a cardinality set by hand stay as they are. Then adjust what is needed and **Save**. Picking the preset again fills the model once more.

---

## Things to know

| Situation | What happens | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| An entity is not linked to the hub. | **Save** is refused and names the entities left out. | Add the missing relation. |
| The entity's query expects parameters. | The explorer runs it without any. | Point the entity at a query without parameters. |
| No column is discovered. | The query failed or returned nothing. | Check the query in Settings → Connectors. |
| A field is missing in the pane. | It is hidden, or the query does not return it. | Untick **Hidden**, or add the column to the query. |

## What's next

- [Analyse data](./analysis.md) — what users do with the model.
- [Roles & permissions](../build/secure/roles-and-permissions.md#access) — give access to a model.

---

## Liberty Next — Analyse data
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/explorer/analysis/

Using the Liberty Next Data Explorer: the fields pane, the Rows, Measures and Filters shelves, the period, Top N, the table, pivot, bar, line, pie and KPI views, the detail view, the drill to the rows behind a figure and the record dialog.

The explorer opens from the **compass** in the header. The model picker at the top right switches between the models available; picking an app in the left navigation opens that app's model.

The analysis runs on its own a moment after each change; **Run** runs it again on demand.

---

## Fields pane \{#fields\}

The left pane lists the model's entities — the analysed one opened, the others folded — with their **1..1** or **1..n** badge. In each entity, the dimensions come first, then the **Σ Measures**. The search box filters the fields of every entity.

| Action | Result |
|---|---|
| Click a field | A dimension goes to **Rows**, a measure to **Measures**. |
| Funnel on a field | The field goes to **Filters**. |
| Drag a field | Drops it on the shelf of choice. |
| Double-click an entity | Makes it the **analysed entity** — the one the analysis starts from (the hub by default). The selector at the left of the toolbar does the same. |

Fields already in use are highlighted. **New calculated field**, at the bottom of the pane, opens the [calculated-field editor](./calculated-fields.md).

---

## Shelves \{#shelves\}

| Shelf | Content |
|---|---|
| **Rows** | The dimensions to group by. A date gets a grouping: *Exact value*, *Day*, *Week*, *Month* (the default), *Quarter*, *Year*. In the detail view, this shelf lists the columns shown. |
| **Measures** | One aggregate per chip: *Sum*, *Average*, *Min*, *Max*, *Count*, *Distinct count* for a number; *Count* or *Distinct count* otherwise. **+** adds a row count. A dimension dropped here counts its distinct values. |
| **Filters** | A field, an operator, a value. Text: *contains*, `=`, `≠`, *starts with*, *ends with*, *in*, *is empty*, *is not empty*. Numbers and dates: `=`, `≠`, *between*, `<`, `≤`, `>`, `≥`, *in*, *is empty*, *is not empty*. A field with a list of values offers its values; *in* takes a comma-separated list. |

Chips move by drag within a shelf; the cross removes one. A filter value applies on **Enter** or when leaving the field.

---

## Period and Top N \{#period\}

The **Period** bar appears when the analysed entity has a date field: pick the date field (the entity's default date first), then a preset — *Today*, *Yesterday*, *Last 7 days*, *Last 30 days*, *This month*, *Last month*, *This quarter*, *This year*, *Last year*, *Last 12 months* — or a custom range on the calendar. *All dates* removes the period.

**Top** keeps the first N groups (up to 10,000). The note in the toolbar reads *N group(s) from M row(s)*, and says when the list was cut or when the figures are partial.

---

## Views \{#views\}

The buttons of the toolbar switch the view without running the query again.

| View | Shows |
|---|---|
| **Table** | One row per group, sortable by header. A click on a row drills to its rows. |
| **Pivot** | The rows as a collapsible hierarchy with subtotals, one dimension spread as **Columns** (*Automatic*: the last one), a grand total, and a **Share** — *of parent* or *of total* — beside each value. Subtotals appear only for a sum or a count: a sum of averages means nothing. Toolbar: expand all, collapse all, Excel export. A click on a value drills. |
| **Bars**, **Lines** | The first dimension on the x axis, the second one (or the measures) as **Series**; the top 10 series, the rest folded into *Others*; dates in order, other categories by value; **Stacked** option. |
| **Pie** | The first dimension as slices, top 10 plus *Others*. |
| **KPI** | One card per measure with its total. |
| **Detail** | The rows themselves, 50 per page, with the **Rows** shelf as columns (the analysed entity's fields when empty). |

**Measure** picks the measure of the pivot or the chart (the first one by default).

---

## Drill and record \{#drill\}

A click on a group of the table or on a value of the pivot lists the **rows behind that figure**: the key, the dimensions and the measures' fields of each row. The values of the cell show above the list (*Country: France*, *Stage: Negotiation*); **Back to the analysis** returns to the figures.

In the detail view, and after a drill, a row of an entity linked to a screen opens that screen's **dialog**: the record shows as it does in the screen, and can be edited with the same rights. The analysis refreshes after a save.

---

## Things to know

| Situation | What happens |
|---|---|
| A measure of a 1..n entity next to hub dimensions. | Summed per hub row, without duplicating the hub's rows. |
| Two 1..n entities in the rows. | Refused, with a message: one many-side entity at a time. |
| The note says the figures are partial. | More than 50,000 grouped rows were read: narrow the period or add a filter. |
| A superuser wants to see the query. | The **SQL** button of the toolbar shows the statement and its values. |

## What's next

- [Calculated fields](./calculated-fields.md) — fields of your own.
- [Saved analyses and dashboards](./saved-and-dashboards.md) — keep, share, export.

## Liberty Next — Calculated fields
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/explorer/calculated-fields/

Calculated fields in the Liberty Next Data Explorer: the editor (name, label, expression, field and function pickers, Test), the expression language — arithmetic, comparisons, conditions, in, is empty, date, text and number functions — and how the result type makes a measure or a dimension.

A calculated field computes a value from the other fields: a margin, a weighted amount, a year, a delay in days, a category. It is written in a small expression language that the server checks and translates for the database — never free SQL. It belongs to the analysis and is saved with it.

---

## At a glance

---

## The editor \{#editor\}

**New calculated field**, at the bottom of the fields pane, opens the editor; the pencil of a calculated field edits it, the bin deletes it (it also leaves the shelves).

| Field | Use |
|---|---|
| **Name** | A letter, then letters, digits or `_`; unique in the analysis. |
| **Label** | The name shown in the pane and the results. |
| **Insert a field**, **Insert a function** | Insert at the cursor; a function is inserted with its arguments selected. |
| **Expression** | The formula. |
| **Test** | Compiles the expression on the server and shows its type and eight sample values. |

**Save** is enabled once the test passes. The result type decides the field's role: a **number** becomes a measure, anything else a dimension. The field then appears in a *calc* group of the pane, and can be used in the rows, the measures and the filters like any other.

---

## The language \{#language\}

A field is written by its name for the analysed entity (`AMOUNT`), or `entity.NAME` for another one (`customers.COUNTRY`). Text values go between single quotes.

| Element | Forms |
|---|---|
| Arithmetic | `+` `-` `*` `/` and brackets. A division by zero gives an empty value. |
| Comparison | `=` `!=` `<>` `<` `<=` `>` `>=` |
| Logic | `and`, `or`, `not` |
| Condition | `condition ? value_if_true : value_if_false` |
| List | `x in ('FR', 'BE')` |
| Empty | `x is empty`, `x is not empty` |
| Dates | `year(d)`, `month(d)`, `day(d)`, `days(from, to)` — the days between two dates |
| Numbers | `round(x, n)`, `abs(x)` |
| Text | `upper(s)`, `lower(s)`, `length(s)`, `concat(a, b, …)` |
| Any | `coalesce(a, b, …)` — the first non-empty value |

A yes/no result shows as `Y` / `N`. A JD Edwards EnterpriseOne Julian date is converted to a real date before a date function applies.

---

## Examples \{#examples\}

| Need | Expression | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Weighted pipeline | `STAGE = 'Negotiation' ? AMOUNT * 0.6 : AMOUNT * 0.3` | measure |
| Unit price | `AMOUNT / QTY` | measure |
| Closing year | `year(CLOSE_DATE)` | measure — a number; to group by it, prefer the *Year* grouping of the date on **Rows** |
| Days to close | `days(CREATED_ON, CLOSE_DATE)` | measure |
| Size band | `AMOUNT >= 100000 ? 'large' : 'standard'` | dimension |
| Domestic or not | `customers.COUNTRY = 'FR'` | dimension (`Y` / `N`) |

---

## Things to know

| Situation | What happens |
|---|---|
| A type mismatch (`AMOUNT + 'x'`). | The test fails and gives the position of the error. |
| An unknown field. | The test fails and names it. |
| The two branches of `? :` have different types. | The test fails: both must be numbers, or both text, or both dates. |
| An expression over 2,000 characters. | Refused. |

## What's next

- [Analyse data](./analysis.md) — the shelves and views.
- [Saved analyses and dashboards](./saved-and-dashboards.md) — a saved analysis keeps its calculated fields.

## Liberty Next — Saved analyses and dashboards
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/explorer/saved-and-dashboards/

Keeping Data Explorer work in Liberty Next: saved analyses, private or shared, with an audience; dashboards of saved analyses with their own period and layout; Excel and PDF export; the analyses and dashboards an app ships.

The mode bar at the top of the explorer has two modes: **Analyses**, the editor with its saved analyses, and **Dashboards**, grids of saved analyses. Each mode shows how many items it holds.

---

## At a glance

---

## Saved analyses \{#analyses\}

In **Analyses** mode, the picker lists the saved analyses of the model, grouped by audience, the user's own ones flagged *mine*. *New analysis* starts an empty one.

| Button | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Save** | Saves the current analysis — rows, measures, filters, period, view, calculated fields. |
| **Save as** | Saves a copy under a new name, always private to start with. |
| **Delete** | Shown to the owner of the analysis and to superusers. |
| **Excel**, **PDF** | Export — see [below](#export). |

The save window asks for:

| Field | Use |
|---|---|
| **Name** | The name in the picker. |
| **Description** | Free text. |
| **Audience** | A group for the picker: *finance*, *sales*, *it*… |
| **Visible to everyone** | Off: private to its owner. On: **shared** — every user who has access to the model sees it. |

Saving a shared analysis changes it for everyone; the window says so. **Save as** makes a personal copy instead.

---

## Dashboards \{#dashboards\}

In **Dashboards** mode, a dashboard is a grid of **tiles**, four columns wide, each running one saved analysis in its own view — table, pivot, chart, KPI or detail.

- **The period** at the top applies to every tile whose analysis has a period field; the others keep theirs.
- **Edit layout** shows the tile tools: move left or right, width (1 to 4 columns), height (*s*, *m*, *l*), remove. **Add an analysis…** adds a tile.
- **The pencil** of a tile opens its analysis in the editor; a drill from a tile does the same, with the clicked values as filters.
- **Save**, **Save as**, **Delete** work as for analyses. A tile whose analysis was deleted says so.

---

## Export \{#export\}

**Excel** and **PDF** export the current analysis, or the whole dashboard (one section per tile):

| | Excel | PDF |
|---|---|---|
| Layout | One sheet per section, bold headers and subtotals, period and filters as a note. | A title, one chapter per section, tables with bold group rows, the install's PDF branding. |
| A pivot | Flattened, with its subtotals. | Same. |
| A chart | Its data table. | Same. |
| KPI | A row of totals. | Same. |
| Detail | Its rows. | Same. |

Each section holds up to 3,000 rows. The pivot view also has its own Excel button, which exports the pivot as shown. PDF branding is set in [Settings → App](../build/settings-app.md).

---

## Analyses shipped with an app \{#bundled\}

An app can ship ready-made analyses and dashboards with its model. They appear as **shared** items when the app is installed, and are updated with new versions of the app — until someone saves changes to them, after which the local version is kept. A shipped item that a user deleted is not installed again.

---

- [Data Explorer](./overview.md) — the whole picture.

## Liberty Next — Secure — overview
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/build/secure/overview/

The security of a Liberty Next install: who can sign in (local users, OpenID Connect, sign-in throttle), what they can open (roles, allow and deny permissions), which rows they see (data scope), how secrets are stored (ENC: values), and the licence.

| Question | Answer | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Who can sign in? | Local users (`auth.toml`, or database tables) and, optionally, OpenID Connect. | [Sign-in](./sign-in.md), [Users](./users.md) |
| What can they open? | Roles made of allow and deny permissions, edited on the application's menu tree. | [Roles and permissions](./roles-and-permissions.md) |
| Which rows do they see? | A role's data scope — by company, region or any dictionary item, possibly from the user's attributes. | [Data scope](./roles-and-permissions.md#data-scope) |
| How are secrets stored? | Encrypted `ENC:` values, with the install's master key. | [Encrypted secrets](./encrypted-secrets.md) |
| Which products are unlocked? | The licence key. | [Licence key](./license-key.md) |

---

## Identity \{#identity\}

| Backend | Users and roles stored in |
|---|---|
| `toml` (default) | `config/auth.toml` — no database needed to sign in. |
| `db` | The `ly2_users`, `ly2_roles` and `ly2_user_roles` tables of the framework pool. |

Either can be combined with **OpenID Connect**: users sign in at the company's identity provider and are created at their first sign-in, without roles; an administrator assigns them. Attributes for the data scope can come from the provider's claims.

Local passwords are hashed (Argon2id). After ten failed sign-ins in five minutes for a user, sign-in is refused for a while (*429*).

---

## Authorization \{#authorization\}

A permission is a colon-separated string — `sql:sales:orders_get`, `api:crm:get_customer`, `menu:sales:orders`, `dashboard:sales.overview`, `ai:chat` — and a role is a list of them, allows and denies (`!…`). The role editor writes them from the menu tree.

| Surface | Checked |
|---|---|
| Run a screen's read query, write a row | `sql:<connector>:<query>` of that query, then the data scope. |
| Call an API endpoint | `api:<connector>:<endpoint>`. |
| See a menu entry | The permission of what the entry runs, or an explicit `menu:` allow; a `menu:` or `dashboard:` deny hides it. |
| Use the assistant | `ai:chat`; the assistant's queries are filtered by the data scope. |
| Settings, Monitoring, Nomaflow, change packages | **Superuser** only. |

A deny wins over an allow, across all of a user's roles; superusers pass every check and every data scope.

---

## Sessions \{#sessions\}

A sign-in gives an access token (one hour) and a refresh token (14 days). Each renewal consumes the refresh token, reads the user again and applies changed roles, attributes or a deactivation. A change of rights therefore reaches a signed-in user within the hour, or at once after signing out and in.

---

## Secrets \{#secrets\}

Pool passwords, API credentials, the licence key, the AI key, the OIDC secret and the SMTP password are encrypted when saved from Settings. The master key that encrypts them comes from the environment and must never change on an existing install. See [Encrypted secrets](./encrypted-secrets.md).

---

## Not provided by the framework \{#not-provided\}

| Need | Where to handle it |
|---|---|
| Multi-factor authentication, password policies | The OpenID Connect provider. |
| Mapping the provider's groups to roles | Not provided: roles are assigned in Settings → Access. |
| Revoking one session at once | Deactivate the user (effective at the next renewal, within the hour); changing the JWT secret signs everybody out. |
| LDAP sign-in | Through an OpenID Connect provider in front of the directory. |

---

## Liberty Next — Sign-in — local and OIDC
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/build/secure/sign-in/

Local users, optional OIDC sign-in against any compliant provider (Keycloak, Azure AD, Auth0, Okta…). What the user sees at sign-in.

A user signs into Liberty through one of two paths:

| Path | When |
|---|---|
| **Local username + password** | The user types credentials on the sign-in screen. The framework checks them against the stored users and mints a JWT. |
| **OIDC** | The user clicks *Sign in with OIDC*, is redirected to the IdP, signs in there, and returns to Liberty with their identity. The framework provisions / updates the user and mints a JWT. |

Both can coexist — a single install offers both buttons on the sign-in screen, and users pick whichever applies.

---

## The sign-in screen

When OIDC is configured, a second button appears below the local form. When OIDC isn't configured, only the local form shows.

---

## Step 1 — Local users

Local users and roles are managed in **Settings → Access**. The installation chooses where they are stored (the server's configuration folder, or the framework's database for several instances sharing one user list); the screens are the same either way.

### Bootstrap the first user

On a fresh install with no users, run:

```bash
liberty-admin init-db
```

The command creates the `admin` superuser and prints a random password once (`--admin-username`, `--password-env` to choose them). The Docker installation runs it for you. Sign in once, then use *Settings → Access → Users* to add others (see [Users](./users.md)).

---

## Step 2 — Configure OIDC (optional) \{#oidc\}

OIDC is layered on top of the local users. Any OIDC-compliant provider works — Liberty discovers endpoints, JWKS and supported scopes from the provider's `.well-known/openid-configuration`.

| Provider | Discovery URL pattern |
|---|---|
| **Keycloak** | `https://<host>/realms/<realm>/.well-known/openid-configuration` |
| **Azure AD** | `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration` |
| **Auth0** | `https://<tenant>.auth0.com/.well-known/openid-configuration` |
| **Okta** | `https://<tenant>.okta.com/oauth2/default/.well-known/openid-configuration` |
| **Google** | `https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration` |

### Configuration

OIDC is set in **Settings → App → OpenID Connect (SSO)**. The client secret is encrypted when saved, in a masked input with an eye to show it. Saving applies the change at once — **no restart**; the next sign-in uses it.

| Field | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Enabled** | yes | Shows or hides the **Sign in with OIDC** button. |
| **Discovery URL** | yes | The provider's `.well-known/openid-configuration` URL. |
| **Client ID** | yes | The client id registered at the provider. |
| **Client secret** | yes | Encrypted when saved. |
| **Scopes** | yes | At least `openid`; `email` and `profile` bring those claims (`openid email profile` by default). |
| **Username claim** | no | The claim that becomes the Liberty user name (`preferred_username` by default; then `email`, then `sub` when absent). |
| **Email claim**, **Name claim** | no | The claims that fill the e-mail address and the full name. |
| **Redirect URL override (proxy)** | no | Only behind a reverse proxy that rewrites the host. |
| **Frontend redirect** | no | Only for a front end that handles the tokens itself. |

See [App settings → OpenID Connect](../settings-app.md#section-4--openid-connect-sso).

### Register the redirect URL with the provider

The redirect URL Liberty expects is:

```
https://<your-framework-host>/auth/oidc/callback
```

Add it to the OAuth2 client's *Redirect URIs* in the provider's console. Without this, the provider rejects the callback with `redirect_uri_mismatch`.

---

## Step 3 — What happens on OIDC sign-in

1. User clicks **Sign in with OIDC** on the sign-in screen.
2. Liberty redirects to the provider's authorization endpoint (`/auth/oidc/login`).
3. User signs in at the provider — including MFA, password resets, all the IdP's own flows.
4. The provider redirects back to `https://<host>/auth/oidc/callback?code=…&state=…`.
5. Liberty exchanges the code for an ID token, validates the signature via JWKS, extracts the claims.
6. Liberty **provisions** or **updates** the local user:
   - First sign-in: a new user row is created with `provider = "oidc"`, `provider_subject = <sub>`, `username = <username_claim>`, `email`, `full_name` from claims. `is_active = true`, **no roles**.
   - Subsequent sign-ins: the email + full name fields are refreshed from the latest claims; roles stay as configured in Liberty.
7. Liberty mints its own JWT pair (access + refresh) and the user is signed in.

The provider's tokens are **not propagated** — Liberty issues fresh tokens with its own signing key. The provider's session ends; Liberty's begins.

---

## OIDC users in the Access page

OIDC users **appear in *Settings → Access → Users* only after their first sign-in** — Liberty doesn't pre-create them. So the typical onboarding pattern is:

1. The new hire signs in via OIDC. They land with no roles → they see an empty app.
2. The operator opens *Settings → Access → Users*, finds the new user, assigns the right roles.
3. The user refreshes (or signs back in) and now has access.

For installs with many OIDC users, an automation script can pre-create them via `POST /admin/access/users` so roles are ready at first sign-in — but the standard flow assumes manual role assignment.

See [Users](./users.md) for the assignment UI.

---

## Tokens — the JWT pair

When sign-in succeeds (local or OIDC), Liberty mints two tokens:

| Token | Default lifetime | What it carries |
|---|---|---|
| **Access token** | 1 hour | The user's `username`, roles, permissions, attributes and resolved data scope. Sent on every API call as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. |
| **Refresh token** | 14 days | Used at `POST /auth/refresh` to mint a new access token without re-typing credentials. |

**Refresh tokens are single-use.** Each `POST /auth/refresh` returns a new refresh token and consumes the one presented. The same token presented again more than 60 seconds later (two browser tabs racing) is refused. An API client must store the refresh token of every reply. The renewal also reads the user again: a deactivated user is refused, and changed roles, attributes and data scope apply from that moment.

### Silent refresh

The refresh is **silent** — the operator never sees a "session expired" prompt on an active browser session:

- A **proactive timer** runs the refresh a short window before the access token expires, so the next API call already carries a fresh token.
- Any API call that comes back **401** triggers a refresh-and-retry: Liberty asks the server for a new access token with the refresh token, replays the original request, and returns the result to the caller. The single 401 is transparent to the calling code.
- If the refresh itself is refused (refresh token expired or revoked), the sign-in screen takes over — this is the only path where the user has to re-authenticate.

The two paths are complementary. The proactive timer covers the common case where the session is quiet enough that no request would notice the expiring token; the 401-retry catches the corner case where the timer missed (a paused tab, a device coming out of sleep). Together they make an active session survive the access token's TTL without visible interruption.

---

## Too many failed sign-ins \{#throttle\}

After 10 failed sign-ins for one username within 5 minutes, `/auth/login` answers *429 — Too many failed logins — try again in N s* until the window has passed. From one client address the limit is five times higher. A successful sign-in clears the count for that user.

The counts are kept in the server's memory: a restart clears them.

---

## Sign-out

Sign-out is **client-side only** — the access token is removed from local storage and the user redirects to the sign-in screen. The token itself remains valid until its TTL expires (it just can't be re-presented without the storage).

For OIDC installs that want **provider sign-out** (terminate the IdP session too), point the provider's *Post-logout redirect URI* at Liberty and configure the provider's end-session endpoint. Liberty doesn't initiate provider logout itself.

---

## Common pitfalls

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| The redirect URL registered at the provider differs from Liberty's. | Sign-in returns `redirect_uri_mismatch`. | Register the exact URL Liberty sends — including the scheme and port. |
| The **Discovery URL** returns 404 or HTML. | Sign-in fails at startup with a config error. | Verify the URL — most providers add `/.well-known/openid-configuration` to a base URL; Liberty needs the full path. |
| The **Username claim** is not in the token. | First sign-in fails with "no username". | Either change the claim to one the IdP actually emits (`email` works for most) or configure the IdP to emit the expected claim. |
| OIDC user signs in but sees an empty app. | Expected — OIDC users land with no roles. | Operator assigns roles via *Settings → Access → Users*. |
| OIDC configured but not enabled. | The OIDC button doesn't show. | Tick **Enabled**. |

---

## What's next

- [Users](./users.md) — add local users, manage OIDC users post-first-sign-in, assign roles.
- [Roles and permissions](./roles-and-permissions.md) — what to assign once a user has signed in.
- [Concepts → Authentication](./sign-in.md) — the deep reference.

## Liberty Next — Roles and permissions
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/build/secure/roles-and-permissions/

Liberty Next roles: what a role grants, edited on the application's own menu tree (inherit / allow / deny per folder or entry, sidebar preview), the rules beyond the menus, and the data scope that restricts which rows a role sees — by company, by any dictionary item, from a user attribute.

A role answers two questions: **what** its holders may open (menus, queries, dashboards, the assistant) and **which rows** they see. Users receive roles; a user with several roles gets the sum of them.

Roles are edited in **Settings → Access → Roles**. The role list is on the left; the selected role opens in a panel with two tabs: **Access** and **Data scope**.

:::info[JD Edwards roles]
This page is about the roles of Liberty Next itself. JD Edwards EnterpriseOne roles and their security are managed in Nomajde.
:::

---

## At a glance

---

## The Access tab \{#access\}

### Baseline

| Choice | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **No access** | Nothing, plus what you allow below. |
| **Full access** | Everything, minus what you deny below. The role card shows a **Full access** tag. |

### The menu tree

The **Menus** block shows the sidebar of every application, one block per application (`sales · 4 of 6 shown`). Each folder and each entry has a three-state control:

| Control | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Inherit** (–) | The node takes the state of its folder, or the baseline. The row says *inherits: allowed* / *denied* / *no access*. |
| **Allow** (✓) | The node and everything under it are granted. |
| **Deny** (⊘) | The node and everything under it are refused, even if another rule would grant them. |

A folder cascades to its children; a child can override it. An entry shows, in grey, what it runs (`sql:sales:orders_get`, a dashboard…): allowing the entry grants both the menu entry and what it runs. The **eye** on each entry previews the result: green, the entry appears in the holder's sidebar; crossed out, it does not.

Two typical roles:

- *Everything except the Security folder*: **Full access**, then **Deny** on the Security folder.
- *Only the Reports folder*: **No access**, then **Allow** on the Reports folder.

### Beyond the menus

Some rights are not tied to a menu entry. The **Beyond the menus** block adds them as green (allow) or red (deny) chips: pick **Allow** or **Deny**, the type, the item, then **Add**.

| Type | Grants |
|---|---|
| Connector (all queries) | Every query of a connector. |
| Query | One query — for a screen reached from a button or a link rather than from the menu. |
| API endpoint | One endpoint of an API connector. |
| Dashboard | One dashboard. |
| Data Explorer | One explorer model, or every model of an app — see [Data Explorer](../../explorer/overview.md#access). |
| AI assistant | The assistant. |
| Pattern (expert) | A permission written by hand, such as `sql:sales:report_*`. |

**Save** writes the role; **Cancel** drops the changes. The role name cannot be changed after creation.

---

## Data scope — which rows \{#data-scope\}

The **Data scope** tab restricts the rows a role sees, on every screen, export, dashboard, report and assistant answer that reads a SQL connector. A role without any rule sees every row.

### A rule

| Field | Choice |
|---|---|
| **Dictionary item** or **Column name** | What to restrict. A dictionary item (`CO — Company`) reaches every column that carries it, in every query; a column name restricts that column only. |
| **Connector** | *Any connector*, or one connector — the rule then says nothing about the others. |
| **Fixed values** or **From the user's attribute** | The allowed values, picked from the item's list when it has one; or a user attribute (`company`), so that one role serves every company — each user carries their own value (see [Users](./users.md#attributes)). |
| **Exclude these values instead** | Turns the list into exclusions: `SY not in 00`. Empty values stay visible. |
| **A query without this item** | *is unrestricted*: a query that has no such column is not limited by this rule. *returns nothing*: such a query returns no row for this role (tag **deny if absent**). |

Each rule appears as one line: `Company (CO) in 00001, 00050`, `SY not in 00`, `Company (CO) = user.company`. Clicking a line loads it in the form; the bin removes it. Rules are saved with the role.

### How rules combine

- Within a role, rules add up: *company in 00001* **and** *SY not in 00*.
- Across a user's roles, the most open role wins: a user holding *subsidiary* and *group* sees what *group* sees.
- A role without rules removes every restriction for its holders.
- Superusers are never restricted.

### Where it applies

- **Reads**: every query of a SQL connector is filtered on the server, whatever calls it — screens, exports, dashboards, reports, the assistant.
- **Writes**: creating, changing or deleting a row outside the scope is refused (*403*).
- Not filtered: API connectors and Nomaflow jobs, which run without a user.

### Finding the column of an item

A query column carries a dictionary item when the screen says so, when it has the item's name, or — on a connector with a **Dd Prefix** (JD Edwards: `2`) — when its name without the table prefix is the item: `ABCO`, `MCCO` and `SDCO` all carry `CO`. A join of two tables restricts both columns. On a pool that trims fixed-length text (JD Edwards), values are compared trimmed.

### When a change takes effect

The scope is computed at sign-in and travels with the session. A change of role or of user attribute applies when the session is renewed — within the hour, or at once after signing out and in. The **Profile** window shows a user their attributes and their data scope in words.

### Without the editor

The same rules can be set with `liberty-admin set-scope` and `set-attributes` ([CLI](../../../references/cli.md#liberty-admin)), or in `auth.toml`:

```toml title="auth.toml"
[roles.subsidiary]
permissions = ["menu:sales:*", "sql:sales:*"]
scope = [
  { dd = "CO", source = "#USER.company#", mode = "deny" },
  { dd = "SY", values = ["00"], exclude = true },
]
```

---

## How permissions are checked \{#resolution\}

Every permission is a colon-separated string — `menu:sales:orders`, `sql:sales:orders_get`, `dashboard:sales_overview`, `ai:chat` — and the editor writes them for you. For a request, Liberty Next takes all the permissions of all the user's roles, then:

1. a superuser is always allowed;
2. a matching **deny** refuses — a deny in one role wins over an allow in another;
3. a matching **allow** grants;
4. otherwise, refused.

`*` matches one segment, or everything when it ends the string (`sql:sales:*`).

---

## Common pitfalls \{#pitfalls\}

| Situation | Explanation |
|---|---|
| A user still sees a menu after its role changed | The session carries the rights: sign out and in, or wait for the renewal (within the hour). |
| A deny meant for one role blocks another | Denies apply across all the user's roles. Prefer *No access* plus allows for narrow roles. |
| A query of the role returns nothing | A rule in *returns nothing* mode, and the query has no column carrying the item. Use *is unrestricted* or add the column. |
| A user with an attribute rule sees nothing | The user has no value for the attribute — see [Users](./users.md#attributes). |
| Roles cannot be deleted from the editor | Remove the role from its users; an unused role grants nothing. |

---

## Liberty Next — Users
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/build/secure/users/

The Settings → Access → Users tab — add local users, manage OIDC users that landed at first sign-in, assign roles, toggle is_active and is_superuser, reset passwords.

A **user** in Liberty is the identity that signs in and carries roles. The Settings → Access → Users tab is where you create local users, see OIDC users that have signed in at least once, assign roles, and toggle the active and superuser flags.

The same UI manages both identity backends (TOML / DB) and both identity sources (local / OIDC). The differences land on **what fields are editable**: OIDC users have no password (it's at the IdP), and their `provider` field is read-only.

---

## The Users tab

Each card shows the username (monospace), full name, email, provider (local / oidc), the status chips and the assigned roles.

| Chip | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **superuser** (orange) | `is_superuser = true` — bypasses every permission check. |
| **inactive** (red) | `is_active = false` — the user can't sign in. Their existing sessions stop on next token refresh. |
| **No roles** (muted) | No roles assigned and not a superuser — the user signs in but sees nothing. |
| **Role names** (purple) | Each assigned role, one chip per role. |

---

## Add a local user

Click **＋ Add user**. The User editor opens with every field empty.

### Fields

| Field | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Username** | yes | Letters, digits, underscores, dots and hyphens. Used as the sign-in handle, the JWT subject, and the audit identity. **Immutable** after creation. |
| **Full name** | no | The display name shown in headers and audit columns. |
| **Email** | no | Recipient address for invites, password reset (when implemented), notification routes. |
| **Password** | yes (for new users) | At least 8 characters. Stored as an Argon2id hash, never readable back. Leave blank on edit to keep the current password. |
| **Roles** | no | Chip picker — type or pick from the dropdown. The dropdown lists every role configured under the Roles tab. |
| **Active** | yes (default on) | When off, the user can't sign in; existing sessions die on next token refresh. |
| **Superuser** | no | When on, bypasses every permission check and every data scope. Use sparingly. |
| **Data-scope attributes** | no | Key / value pairs read by the roles' data scope — see [below](#attributes). |

Click **Save** — the user is created and the modal closes. The new user appears at the top of the list.

### Endpoints behind the scenes

| Action | Endpoint |
|---|---|
| Create | `POST /admin/access/users` |
| Update | `PATCH /admin/access/users/{username}` |
| Password change | `POST /admin/access/users/{username}/password` |

The TOML backend writes to `config/auth.toml` atomically; the DB backend commits to `ly2_users` / `ly2_user_roles`. Either way, the change takes effect immediately — the user can sign in with the new password right away.

---

## Edit an existing user

Click any user row to open the editor with their current values:

| Field | Editable | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Username** | no | Pinned at creation. |
| **Full name** / **Email** | yes | Update freely. |
| **Password** | yes (local users only) | Leave blank to keep the current password. Typing a new one (8+ chars) sets it on Save. |
| **Roles** | yes | Add / remove chips. |
| **Active** | yes | Toggle to deactivate. |
| **Superuser** | yes | Toggle to grant / revoke superuser. |
| **Data-scope attributes** | yes | See [below](#attributes). |

Saves go through `PATCH /admin/access/users/{username}` for the property updates and `POST /admin/access/users/{username}/password` if a new password was typed.

:::tip[When the user is signed in]
Changes don't break their current session. The new roles / disabled flag / password take effect on the next **refresh** (within the access token TTL — default 1 hour) or **sign-out + sign-in**.
:::

---

## Data-scope attributes \{#attributes\}

A role's [data scope](./roles-and-permissions.md#data-scope) can take its values from the user instead of listing them: a rule *Company (CO) = user.company* lets one role serve every subsidiary, each user seeing their own companies.

In the user form, **Data-scope attributes** holds one row per attribute: a key (`company`) and a value (`00001, 00050` — a comma makes a list). **Add an attribute…** suggests the keys the roles already use. A user who lacks the attribute a rule needs sees no row through that rule.

The users list shows the attributes on each card (`company=00001,00050`), and the user sees them, with their data scope in words, in their **Profile** window. From the command line: `liberty-admin set-attributes alice company=00001,00050`.

---

## OIDC users — the differences

OIDC users land in the Users list **after their first sign-in** — Liberty auto-creates them with `provider = "oidc"`. The editor for an OIDC user looks the same, but:

| Field | Editable for OIDC? | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Username** | no | Same as local. |
| **Full name** / **Email** | technically yes, but… | On every OIDC sign-in, these fields are **refreshed from the IdP claims**. Manual edits get overwritten. Edit them at the IdP instead. |
| **Password** | no | The IdP holds the password. The field is disabled or rejected with HTTP 400. |
| **Roles** | yes | This is the main reason operators visit OIDC users — to assign roles. |
| **Active** | yes | When off, sign-in is rejected even with valid OIDC tokens. |
| **Superuser** | yes | Toggle to grant the bypass. |

The standard onboarding sequence:

1. The new hire signs in via OIDC for the first time.
2. They land with **no roles** → they see an empty app.
3. They tell their admin "I'm in but see nothing".
4. The admin opens *Settings → Access → Users*, finds them, assigns the right roles, saves.
5. The user refreshes the page (or signs out + back in) and now has access.

For installs that want to pre-create OIDC users with roles already attached, scripts can hit `POST /admin/access/users` with `provider = "oidc"` and the expected `provider_subject` (the `sub` claim). On first sign-in the framework finds the pre-created user and uses it. Standard installs skip this and assign roles after first sign-in.

---

## Deactivating a user \{#deactivate\}

Users are not deleted: to take someone out, switch **Active** off and save. They can no longer sign in; their current session ends when its access token expires (one hour at most), since the renewal is refused. Roles, attributes and history are kept, and switching **Active** back on restores the account as it was.

---

## What you actually do — typical workflows

### Onboard a local hire

1. *Settings → Access → Users → ＋ Add user*.
2. Username = corporate handle, password = a one-time string they'll change, email = their address.
3. Assign roles per their team (`analyst`, `reporter`, …).
4. Save.
5. Send them the temporary credentials through whatever channel your company uses.
6. They sign in, they reach the AI assistant or change-password flow to set their own password.

### Onboard an OIDC hire

1. They sign in via OIDC the first time — Liberty auto-creates the account.
2. They report no access.
3. *Settings → Access → Users*, find them, assign roles, save.
4. They refresh → they're in.

### Change a user's password (you're the admin)

1. *Settings → Access → Users*, click the user.
2. Type the new password in the **Password** field (8+ chars).
3. Save.
4. Tell the user. They sign in with the new password; their existing session keeps working until the access token expires.

### Revoke an account immediately

1. Toggle **Active** off and save.
2. If you can't tolerate the up-to-1-hour delay until their current access token expires, rotate the JWT signing secret (`LIBERTY_JWT_SECRET`) and restart. Every existing token is invalidated — a heavy hammer but the only **immediate** revocation Liberty offers.

---

## Common pitfalls

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| OIDC user has no roles after sign-in. | Expected — the operator hasn't assigned any yet. | Open *Settings → Access → Users*, assign roles. |
| Editing an OIDC user's email reverts on next sign-in. | The IdP claim wins; the framework refreshes from the latest token. | Edit the email at the IdP. |
| Trying to set a password for an OIDC user. | Backend rejects with 400. | OIDC users have no local password — they sign in through the provider. |
| Changing a user's role doesn't take effect immediately. | The user's JWT still has the old roles. | They refresh (or sign-out + sign-in) — within the access token TTL the new roles apply. |
| A user with an attribute-based scope sees nothing. | The user has no value for the attribute the rule reads. | Add it under **Data-scope attributes**. |
| Marking a user superuser to fix a permission gap. | Works, but bypasses every check — including ones the user shouldn't be bypassing. | Add the missing permission to one of their roles instead. |

---

## Liberty Next — Encrypted secrets
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/build/secure/encrypted-secrets/

How Liberty Next stores pool passwords, API credentials, the licence key, the AI key, the OIDC client secret and the SMTP password: encrypted as ENC: values on every save from Settings, with the install's master key.

Every secret field of Settings is encrypted when it is saved and written to the configuration file as `ENC:…`. The server decrypts it when it loads the file, with the install's **master key**.

| Field | Settings |
|---|---|
| Pool password | Settings → Pools |
| API connector credentials (password, token, client secret) | Settings → Connectors |
| Licence key, Anthropic API key, OIDC client secret, SMTP password | Settings → App |

A secret field is a masked input with an eye to show its content. There is nothing to switch on: a value saved from Settings is always encrypted, and the save is refused when the server has no master key.

To give a secret from the environment instead, write `${VARIABLE}` in the file; to write an `ENC:` value by hand, use `liberty-crypto encrypt`. The details — the key, its derivation, `<NAME>_FILE` secrets — are on [Encryption & secrets](../../configuration/encryption-secrets.md).

:::warning[The master key]
Keep a copy of the master key outside the server and never change it on an existing install: every `ENC:` value would become unreadable. `./liberty doctor` checks that it decrypts every pool password.
:::

---

## Liberty Next — License key
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/build/secure/license-key/

The Liberty Next licence key: what it unlocks (Nomasx-1, Nomajde), where to paste it (Settings → App → License), how to check it (liberty-license, /api/license), what happens without it, and how to replace it before it expires.

The framework is free to use. The licensed applications — **Nomasx-1** and **Nomajde** — are unlocked by a licence key delivered by Nomana-IT.

---

## At a glance

---

## Install the key \{#install\}

Sign in as a superuser, open **Settings → App → License**, paste the key into **License key** and save. The key is encrypted with the install's master key, and the licensed applications load at once — no restart.

Before pasting it, the key can be checked from the server: `liberty-license verify <key>` (on Docker: `docker exec -u liberty liberty-next liberty-license verify <key>`).

---

## Check the licence \{#check\}

| Where | Shows |
|---|---|
| The **License** section header | *configured*, or *not set — restricted mode*. |
| `liberty-license status` | Validity, products covered, expiry date of the configured key. |
| `GET /api/license` | `{mode, customer, plan, apps, expires_at, error}`. |
| `GET /info` | `license.mode`: `full` or `restricted`. |

---

## Without a valid key \{#restricted\}

Without a key, or with an expired or invalid one, the server runs in **restricted mode**: the framework and the applications built on it work, the licensed applications do not load. The server log says why with a line starting `license: not loading licensed connector(s)`.

---

## Replace the key \{#replace\}

Note the expiry date when the key is installed. Before it expires, paste the new key in **Settings → App → License** and save: it applies at once.

The key can also come from the environment variable `LIBERTY_LICENSE_KEY`, for installs that keep secrets in an orchestrator; Settings then shows the reference as it is.

---

## Liberty Next — App settings
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/build/settings-app/

Settings → App in Liberty Next: the six sections — App (name, address, logs, language, UI defaults, hot reload, Oracle thick mode), License, AI Assistant, Notifications (email), OpenID Connect (SSO), PDF branding — what each field does, which secrets are encrypted, and what needs a restart.

**Settings → App** holds the application settings. Each section folds; its header shows a summary (*configured*, *not set — restricted mode*, *no API key*, *disabled*…). **Save** validates and applies the whole page at once. The editor is in English.

Secret fields — the licence key, the Anthropic API key, the SMTP password, the OIDC client secret — are masked inputs with an eye; they are encrypted with the master key when saved ([Encryption](../configuration/encryption-secrets.md)).

---

## At a glance

---

## App \{#app\}

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| **App name** | The application's name. |
| **Bind host**, **Port** | Listening address and port. **Restart needed.** |
| **Log level** | `debug`, `info`, `warning`, `error`, `critical`. **Restart needed.** |
| **Default language** | Labels when a request names no language. |
| **Default period (dashboards)** | The preset a dashboard opens on when it names none — see [Dashboards](../dashboards.md#period). |
| **Grid page size** | The grids' initial page size (10 to 10 000, default 50). A saved view's own size wins. |
| **Dashboard cache (seconds, 0 = none)** | How long a reopened dashboard reuses its widgets' results (default 60). |
| **Hot-reload config TOML files on change** | Apply configuration files as soon as they change — see [Hot reload](../configuration/hot-reload.md). |
| **Oracle thick mode (…)** | Oracle Instant Client for every Oracle pool — needed for Native Network Encryption and LOBs over a database link. Takes effect after a restart. See [Connectors](../connectors.md#oracle-thick). |

When a saved change needs a restart, the page says *Saved. Restart the server to apply the new settings.*

## License \{#license\}

**License key**: paste the key delivered by Nomana-IT. The licensed connectors load at once, without a restart. See [Licence key](./secure/license-key.md).

## AI Assistant \{#ai\}

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Enabled** | The assistant answers; users need the `ai:chat` permission. |
| **Anthropic API key** | Without it, the assistant says it is not configured. |
| **Model**, **Effort**, **Max tokens**, **Adaptive thinking** | The model and how much it reasons and writes. |
| **Max tool iterations** | Tool calls per answer, at most (default 8). |
| **Request timeout (s)** | Default 120. |
| **System prompt** | Empty: the built-in instructions. |
| **Connector tools** | The assistant may list connectors and run their **read** queries. |
| **API tool** | The assistant may call API endpoints — off by default, since an endpoint may change data. |
| **Scaffold tools** | The assistant may propose queries, dictionary entries, screens and menu items; the user applies the proposal. |
| **Allowed connectors** | The connectors the assistant may use; empty means all. |
| **Allowed domains**, **Max fetches per turn** | Web pages the assistant may read; no domain means no web access. |

See [AI assistant](../ai-assistant.md).

**Notifications enabled**, then the **Server** (SMTP host, Port, Encryption — STARTTLS, implicit TLS or none —, Timeout), the **Account** (User, Password) and **Sending** (From address, Keep read notifications — days, `0` = forever). See [Notifications](../../nomaflow/notifications.md#smtp).

## OpenID Connect (SSO) \{#section-4--openid-connect-sso\}

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|

| **Client ID**, **Client secret**, **Scopes** | As registered at the provider (`openid email profile` by default). |
| **Username claim**, **Email claim**, **Name claim** | Which ID-token claims fill the user (`preferred_username`, `email`, `name`). |

Register `https://<host>/auth/oidc/callback` as redirect URI at the provider. See [Sign-in](./secure/sign-in.md#oidc).
